questions.source: LAND4.2: Title to land: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A company is taking a 15-year lease of a shop unit. The freehold title is unregistered. The lawyer acting for the freeholder states that their client will not produce evidence of title, as it is not necessary. Should the company be concerned about the freeholder’s position regarding the title?
options: The company should insist that the freehold title is produced, otherwise the company will only secure a qualified title on registration.
The company need not be concerned – the lease is only 15 years in length and so is not substantively registrable.
The company should insist that the freehold is produced, otherwise the company will only secure a good leasehold title on registration.
The company need not be concerned because title absolute of the leasehold title will be available on registration.
The company should insist that the freehold title is perfected by a voluntary registration.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.2: Title to land: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Person A has received accountancy advice suggesting that they assign their beneficial interest in a piece of freehold land to their daughter. Person A instructs their lawyer, who drafted the deed of assignment which is duly completed. Is the deed of assignment substantively registrable at HM Land Registry?
options: No, the assignment is a legal interest which is not capable of substantive registration at HM Land Registry.
No, HM Land Registry only registers the legal title to the land, not any equitable interests.
Yes, the parties entered into a deed which is substantively registrable at HM Land Registry.
No, HM Land Registry only registers the legal title to the land, not the beneficial interest.
Yes, the freehold estate is subject to substantive registration at HM Land Registry.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.2: Title to land: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

land4.3.stem: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A lawyer is acting for a developer who is purchasing a detached house on a large plot of land. The lawyer investigates the seller’s title to the land, which is unregistered. The lawyer finds a deed dated 5 September 1968 which contains the following covenant: “Not to build more than one dwelling on the property.” The developer is keen on the property because the garden is big and they want to build two more dwellings on the land. The buyer’s lawyer carries out the appropriate full land charges search and the search comes back with no entries appearing on it. Should the buyer be concerned about the covenant against building more than one dwelling?
options: Yes, because the covenant is contained in a deed so it will bind the buyer.
Yes, because the buyer has notice of the covenant.
No, because the covenant is in a deed dated 5 September 1968 and will not be enforceable.
No, because the covenant is not registered as a D(ii) land charge and is not binding.
No, because the covenant is not registered as a C(iv) land charge and is not binding.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A couple in a civil partnership are splitting-up. One party seeks legal advice because they are worried that their partner wants them to leave the property, which the couple have lived in as their home. The lawyer discovers that the title to the property is unregistered and that their client is not a legal owner of the property. What advice should the lawyer give to their client to protect their position?
options: The lawyer should register a class F land charge in favour of their client against the name of the legal owner of the property.
The client has an overriding interest so their interest is protected.
The lawyer should register a notice against the charges register of the title to the property.
The client has the right to occupy the property because they have lived in it as their home and no further steps should be taken.
The client has no interest to protect because they are not married to the legal owner of the property.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A buyer contracts to buy a piece of unregistered land. Completion is due to take place in five months. Which of the following describes how the contract should be protected?
options: As a class F land charge.
It does not need protection.
As a D(ii) land charge.
As a C(i) land charge.
As a C(iv) land charge.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A lawyer acts for the seller of a property with an unregistered title. The lawyer's investigation of title reveals that the property is subject to a charge in favour of a bank dated 8 June 1984, and a charge in favour of a building society dated 15 May 1989. How will the charge dated 8 June 1984 be protected?
options: The charge would be protected by the registration of a class C(iv) land charge.
The charge would be protected by the registration of a class C(i) land charge.
The charge would be protected by the production of an epitome of title.
The charge would be protected because the lender will hold the title deeds as security for the loan.
The charge would be protected by the registration of a charge on the charges register.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A lawyer acts for the seller of a property with an unregistered title. The lawyer's investigation of title reveals that the property is subject to a charge in favour of a bank dated 20 September 1983, and a charge in favour of a building society dated 18 March 1988. How will the charge dated 18 March 1988 be protected?
options: The charge would be protected by the registration of a charge on the charges register.
The charge would be protected by the registration of a class C(i) land charge.
The charge would be protected by the registration of a class C(iv) land charge.
The charge would be protected because the lender will hold the title deeds as security for the loan.
The charge would be protected by the production of an epitome of title.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: In 1987, a landowner sold a field to a buyer by way of a conveyance which included the following covenant: “Not to build more than one dwelling on the property.” The 1987 transaction did not trigger first registration. The buyer has just sold the field to a developer. The developer’s lawyer carried out a full land charges search which revealed a land charge D(ii) entry in relation to the covenant revealed against the buyer’s name. The developer wants to build three houses on the field. Which of the following statements best describes the developer’s position regarding the covenant?
options: The developer is not bound by the covenant because it does not appear on the charges register of title.
The developer is not bound by the covenant because it should have been registered as a class C(iv) land charge.
The developer is bound by the covenant because their lawyer had notice of the covenant by investigating the title.
The developer is bound by the covenant because it was correctly registered as a D(ii) land charge.
The developer is not bound by the covenant because the developer was not a party to the deed which created it.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A buyer completed the purchase of a piece of land with unregistered title last month. Which of the following statements best describes when the legal title will be transferred to the buyer?
options: Legal title passes upon completion.
Legal title passes when the money passes from the buyer to the seller.
Legal title passes once the transfer is registered at HM Land Registry.
Legal title passes once the agreement to buy and sell is made.
Legal title passes upon exchange of contracts.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person’s parents have agreed to lend them £30,000 to assist with developing their business. The parents want to ensure that the £30,000 is repaid to them at some point in the future. The person does not own any business assets but does own a home, which is registered at HM Land Registry in the person’s sole name. What legal advice should the parents receive, regarding their wish to recover the money lent to the person?
options: The parents will not be able to ensure the return of the £30,000 because the person wants it for the person’s business.
The parents should take a legal charge over the person’s home and register it on the charges register of the person’s title.
The parents should ask the person to prepare a will, leaving the £30,000 to them in the event of the person's death.
The parents should put a form A restriction on the proprietorship register of the person’s title.
The parents should take a legal charge over the person’s home and register it on the property register of the title.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A couple in a civil partnership are splitting-up. One of them is concerned that their partner wants them to move out of the property which the couple have lived in as their home. The party consults a lawyer who finds out that the title to the property is unregistered and that their client is not a legal owner of the property. How can the non-owning party protect its position?
options: Their lawyer must register a class C(i) land charge.
Their lawyer must register a class F land charge.
Their lawyer must register a class C(iv) land charge.
Their lawyer must register a class D(ii) land charge.
Their lawyer must register a class D(iii) land charge.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A development company has entered into a contract with a landowner under which it has the right to require the landowner to sell the land to the development company for £350,000 if the development company secures planning permission within 18 months of the date of the contract. The landowner’s title is unregistered. How can the development company protect its interest?
options: By registering a class C(iv) land charge against the landowner’s name.
By registering a class C(i) land charge against the landowner’s name.
By registering a notice on the charges register of the landowner’s title.
By registering a notice on the property register of the landowner’s title.
The development company does not yet have an interest which is capable of protection.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.3: Methods to protect and enforce third party interest: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

land4.4.stem: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Ten years ago, two friends purchased a property together for £80,000. They contributed equally to the purchase price and both appear on the title as registered proprietors. They hold the beneficial interest as joint tenants and did not enter into an agreement regarding the beneficial interest. The property is now being sold for £200,000. How will the sale proceeds be divided?
options: Each party will receive the net sale proceeds in the shares that they agreed at the time of the purchase.
Each party will receive £40,000 and the balance will be placed on trust for them equally.
The sale proceeds will be divided in accordance with a declaration of trust.
Each party will receive £100,000.
One party will receive £120,000, the other will receive £80,000.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Two business partners purchased a freehold shop together five years ago. They contributed equally to the purchase price and both appear on the title as registered proprietors. They initially agreed to hold the beneficial interest as joint tenants. They have received tax advice and now wish to bring the joint tenancy to an end, but wish to remain co-owners. How can the business partners give effect to the tax advice?
options: The joint tenancy in law must be severed and a form A restriction placed on the proprietorship register.
The business partners must enter into a declaration of trust to specify how the beneficial interest is to be held.
The joint tenancy in equity must be severed and a form A restriction placed on the proprietorship register.
The joint tenancy in equity must be severed and a form A restriction placed on the property register.
One partner must transfer their interest in the property to the other by way of gift.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: “A legal mechanism by which if the buyer of land pays the purchase money to two or more trustees, the interest of any behind-the-scenes beneficiary transfers from the land to the proceeds of sale, that is, the money.” What legal process does the above describe?
options: Overreaching.
Co-ownership.
Overriding.
Overarching.
Severance.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Five friends buy a property together. They are all over 18. They each contribute £50,000 towards the purchase price of the property. How will the legal estate be held?
options: The first four of them will hold the legal estate as tenants in common on trust for all of them.
The first four of them named in the transfer deed will hold the legal estate as joint tenants on trust for all of them.
They will all hold the legal estate as joint tenants.
A trust of land will arise automatically.
They will all hold the legal estate as tenants in common.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A married couple co-owned their matrimonial home as joint tenants in law and equity. They were going to get divorced and the husband moved out of the matrimonial home and went to live with his parents. The wife put a notice of severance through the letterbox at the address where the husband was living. She subsequently decided that she would like to get back with her husband and left him a voice message on his mobile telephone, purporting to revoke the notice of severance. Two hours after she left a voicemail, her husband died leaving a will in which he left his entire estate to his sibling. Which answer best describes who is entitled to the husband’s equitable interest in the matrimonial home?
options: It has passed to his sibling due to the doctrine of survivorship.
It has passed to his parents as he was living with them at the date of his death.
It has passed to his sibling because the notice of severance could not be revoked.
It has passed to his wife due to the doctrine of survivorship.
It has passed to his wife because the gift to the husband’s sibling is defeated by a joint tenancy in law and equity.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Two friends buy a house together. One party contributed 80% of the purchase price and the other contributed the remaining 20%. Which of the following statements best describes how they hold their respective legal and equitable interests in the property?
options: They will own the legal estate as joint tenants on trust for themselves as beneficial joint tenants.
They will own the legal estate as joint tenants on trust for themselves as beneficial tenants in common in the shares in which they contributed to the purchase price.
They will own the legal and equitable estates as tenants in common in equal shares.
They will own the legal estate as joint tenants on trust for themselves as beneficial tenants in common in equal shares.
They will own the legal and equitable estates as tenants in common in the shares in which they contributed to the purchase price.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A lawyer is acting for the buyer of a freehold property from two registered proprietors. The buyer is concerned because the seller's parent lives at the property. Although they are not on the register of title, the seller's parent may have contributed to the original purchase of the property. Which of the following statements best describes how the buyer will be protected?
options: Provided that the buyer makes an enquiry of the seller, the buyer need not be concerned about the interest of the seller's parent.
Provided that the purchase money is paid to two trustees, any interest of the seller's parent will be overridden.
Provided that another trustee is appointed in the transfer, any interest of the seller’s parent will be overreached.
Provided that the purchase money is paid to two trustees, any interest of the seller's parent will be overreached.
Provided that the buyer is a bona fide purchaser of the property for value, they need not be concerned.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Five friends buy a property together, each contributing £40,000. Four of the friends are over 18. One is 17 and has just inherited some money from their grandparent and also decides to contribute £40,000 towards the purchase price. How will the legal estate be held?
options: They will all hold the legal estate as tenants in common.
Four of them, including the 17-year-old, will hold the legal estate as joint tenants on trust for all of them.
The four who are over 18 will hold the legal estate as tenants in common on trust for all of them.
They will all hold the legal estate as joint tenants.
The four who are over 18 will hold the legal estate as joint tenants on trust for all of them.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Two business colleagues are going to invest in some commercial premises together. They intend to run their florist business from the premises that they buy. They intend to purchase the freehold jointly. One will contribute £56,000 to the purchase and the other will contribute £10,000. Which of the following statements best describes how they should hold the beneficial interest in the property?
options: They should hold the beneficial interest as tenants in common in equal shares.
They should hold the beneficial interest as joint tenants in common in unequal shares to reflect the inequality of contribution to the purchase price.
They should hold the beneficial interest as tenants in common in unequal shares to reflect the inequality of contribution to the purchase price.
They should hold the beneficial interest as joint tenants and sever it when the florist shop opens.
They should hold the beneficial interest as joint tenants.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A spouse wishes to divorce their partner and visits a matrimonial solicitor for advice. They inform the solicitor that the matrimonial home is registered at HM Land Registry in their joint names. The solicitor obtains a copy of the register of title and notes that there is no restriction registered on the proprietorship register. The spouse instructs the solicitor that they do not want to leave their interest in the property to their partner and will be instructing the law firm to prepare a will for them immediately leaving their interest in the property to their two young children. What step should the spouse's solicitor take to ensure that their instructions can be carried out effectively once the will is concluded?
options: A notice severing the equitable joint tenancy should immediately be served on the husband.
A transfer of the spouse's interest in the property to their children should be concluded.
A notice of severance should be placed on the proprietorship register.
A Form A restriction should be placed on the proprietorship register.
A notice severing the legal joint tenancy should immediately be served on the partner.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.4: Co-ownership and trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A landowner verbally grants a person permission to walk through their woodland so that a person can take photographs and sell the photographs on a person’s online gallery. Which answer best describes the nature of the interest that person holds?
options: A person has an easement as the right is not of limited duration.
A person has a lease as it is not necessary for rent to be paid to create a lease.
A person has an equitable interest as the right has not been created by deed.
A person has a licence as they only have a personal right.
A person has a profit a prendre.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: 12 months ago, a homeowner borrowed £80,000 from a bank to build an extension at their property. The loan is secured by a second legal charge on the charges register of the homeowner’s title. The mortgage contained a clause requiring repayment of the capital after six months. The homeowner defaults on three monthly repayments. Can the bank exercise a power of sale over the property?
options: Yes, if the bank joins the first mortgagee in the possession proceedings.
Yes, provided that six months have elapsed since the homeowner entered into the mortgage.
No, because the power of sale has not become exercisable.
Yes, because the bank has a valid legal charge registered over the charges register of title.
No, because the bank only has a second charge over the property.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A landowner owns a piece of land which is landlocked. The landowner needs to pass over land belonging to their neighbour to gain access to the public highway. What type of interest does the landowner require?
options: A rent charge.
An easement.
A profit a prendre.
A mortgage.
A licence.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A lawyer acting for the buyer of a piece of land with freehold title investigates the title to the land and discovers a clause in the following terms: “Not to allow the fence on the western boundary to fall into disrepair.” What type of clause is this?
options: It is a mortgage.
It is a positive covenant.
It is an easement.
It is a profit a prendre.
It is a restrictive covenant.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The registered proprietor of a property has taken a shortcut to the public highway by walking through their neighbour’s field for the last six years. The neighbour sent a letter asking the registered proprietor to stop walking through their field but the registered proprietor is sure that their property has a right of way over the field. How would a right of way appear on the registered proprietor’s title?
options: It would not matter because the registered proprietor has acquired the right by prescription.
As a restriction on the proprietorship register.
As a restriction on the property register.
A notice on the charges register.
As a notice on the property register.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The registered proprietor of a property has taken a shortcut to the public highway by walking through their neighbour’s field for the last seven years. The neighbour sent a letter asking the registered proprietor to stop walking through their field but the registered proprietor is sure that their property has a right of way over the field. How would a right of way appear on the neighbour’s title?
options: As a restriction on the property register.
It would not matter because the registered proprietor has acquired the right by prescription.
A notice on the charges register.
As a notice on the property register.
As a restriction on the proprietorship register.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: For the last 22 years, a person has driven over their neighbour’s driveway to get to the public highway. The person’s title does not contain reference to the use of their neighbour’s driveway. Over the years, the person has asked their neighbour if they can continue to use the driveway and has made a few payments towards the upkeep of the driveway. The neighbour has just sold their land and the new owner has told the person that they cannot use the driveway any more. Which of the following statements best describes the person’s legal position?
options: The person can demand that the arrangement to use the driveway is formalised in a deed of easement.
The person has a right to use the driveway because he has acquired an easement.
The person has no legal right to use the driveway and has not acquired a right to use it by prescription.
The person has no legal right to use the driveway but has acquired a right to use it by licence.
The person has a prescriptive right to use the driveway.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A bank has agreed to lend a buyer £200,000 for the purchase of a property with registered title. The bank and the buyer will enter into a legal charge. How will the bank’s interest be protected?
options: By a notice on the proprietorship register.
By a restriction on the proprietorship register.
By a restriction on the charges register.
By a notice on the property register.
By a notice on the charges register.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The person has no legal right to use the driveway but has acquired a right to use it by licence. The person has a prescriptive right to use the driveway.
options: The landowner must ensure that the rights are completed by registration to be valid.
The landowner cannot create the rights before the sale because there will not be a dominant and servient tenement in separate ownership.
The landowner need not take any action prior to sale as they can rely on implied easements in equity.
The landowner must ensure that all rights are capable of forming the subject matter of an easement.
The landowner must ensure that the rights are created by deed, otherwise they will only take effect in equity.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A bank has agreed to lend a farmer £100,000 for their business. The farmer owns 110 acres of farmland, the title to which is unregistered. The bank will take a first legal charge over 20 acres of the farmer’s land. How will the bank’s interest be protected?
options: The transaction will trigger first registration of the 20 acres of land and the charge will be protected by a notice on the charges register.
The charge will be protected by the registration of a C(i) land charge in favour of the bank.
The transaction will trigger first registration of the 110 acres of the farm and the charge will be protected by a notice on the charges register.
The charge will be protected by a deposit of the title deeds with the bank as security for the loan.
The transaction will trigger first registration of the 20 acres of land and the charge will be protected by a notice on the property register.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.5: Proprietary rights: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Section 16(3) Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 states: “…(a) By virtue of a covenant against assignment (whether absolute or qualified) the assignment cannot be effected without the consent of the landlord under the tenancy or some other person; (b) any such consent is given subject to a condition (lawfully imposed) that the tenant is to enter into an agreement guaranteeing the performance of the covenant by the assignee; and (c) the agreement is entered into by the tenant in pursuance of that condition.” What document does the above definition describe?
options: An authorised guarantee agreement.
An authorised guarantee agreement. A guarantee indemnity agreement.
A licence to assign.
An authorised guarantor agreement.
A rent deposit deed.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.6_ Leases_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: The tenant of a shop wants to sell the residue of the lease of the premises. The tenant has checked the lease and it contains the following clause: “Not to assign the demised premises without the landlord’s consent.” What is the effect of this clause?
options: The tenant is obliged to seek the landlord's consent to assignment and must make the request in writing.
The landlord cannot withhold their consent to assignment if the incoming tenant is creditworthy.
The landlord cannot withhold their consent to assignment if the outgoing tenant meets the landlord's legal fees.
The landlord can only withhold their consent to assignment if it is reasonable to do so.
The landlord can withhold their consent to assignment in any circumstances.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.6_ Leases_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A and B have entered into a valid written agreement called a “licence to occupy”. Under the terms of the agreement, B can live in the flat for 1 year and will pay A £600 per month for the year. Which of the following best describes the arrangement which A and B have entered into?
options: B’s occupation will be under the terms of a licence because this is the label that has been given to it and the label is conclusive.
B’s occupation will be under the terms of a lease because the arrangement has all of the hallmarks of a lease and the label given to the arrangement is irrelevant.
B’s occupation will be under the terms of a tenancy at will because B has no security of tenure.
B’s occupation will be under the terms of a tenancy at sufferance.
B’s occupation will be under the terms of an equitable lease, as fairness demands that B has a lease.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.6_ Leases_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A landlord creates a lease of its factory premises in favour of a tenant. The lease includes the following provision: “This lease shall expire when the English football team win the World Cup”. Which of the following statements best describes this document?
options: The document has created a valid lease which can be brought to an end by the landlord or the tenant.
The document is an implied periodic tenancy.
The document has created a protected business tenancy.
The document is an equitable lease because the term is uncertain.
The document has not created a lease because it would be void for uncertainty.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.6_ Leases_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A landlord has let a private dwelling to a tenant for 12 months at a rent of £700 per month. The landlord and the tenant entered into a lease. The landlord insists on visiting the tenant, uninvited, at least once a week claiming that they are entitled to check the state and condition of the dwelling. Is the landlord in breach of any of their obligations under the lease?
options: Yes, the landlord is guilty of harassment.
No, the landlord is entitled to peaceable re-entry.
Only if the lease contains a covenant by the landlord for quiet enjoyment.
Yes, the landlord is in breach of the duty of quiet enjoyment.
Yes, the landlord is in breach of the duty of quiet enjoyment. No, a landlord is entitled to enter the demised premises to view the condition of the property.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.6_ Leases_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A commercial lease contains the following provision: “Not to use the demised premises as anything other than office premises without the landlord’s consent.” Due to a downturn in trade, the tenant wants to use the premises as a shop because the tenant believes that this will be more profitable. The tenant applies for the landlord’s consent to the change of use under the lease, but the landlord has refused the consent on the basis that the landlord hates shopping and will only buy goods online. Is the landlord entitled to withhold their consent in this manner?
options: No, because this is a qualified covenant and the landlord cannot unreasonably withhold their consent.
Yes, because the proposed use would damage the landlord’s commercial interests.
No, because withholding consent in this manner is a breach of the landlord’s duty of quiet enjoyment.
Yes, because in relation to change of use with the landlord’s consent, the landlord does not have to act reasonably in refusing.
Yes, because this is an absolute covenant and the landlord is entitled to refuse any request from the tenant.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.6_ Leases_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A landlord and tenant have entered into a lease of commercial premises which includes a landlord covenant to maintain the exterior structure of the building, within which the demised premises are situated, including the roof, external walls and foundations. The tenant is concerned because the roof is leaking which could cause damage to the tenant’s belongings contained in the demised premises. The tenant does not have any spare financial resources and wants the roof to be fixed as soon as possible. Which of the following statements best describes the most appropriate course of action for the tenant?
options: The tenant could set off the cost of repairs against future rent payments.
The tenant could pursue the landlord for repudiation.
The tenant could pursue the landlord for an injunction.
The tenant could pursue the landlord for damages for breach of covenant.
The tenant could pursue the landlord for an order for specific performance.
questions.subject: Land Law
questions.source: LAND4.6_ Leases_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

prop12.1.stem: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: In a conveyancing transaction, the matter progresses towards exchange of contracts. What is the significance of this stage in the contract to a seller and buyer?
options: It is the point in the transaction where the matter becomes legally binding between the seller and buyer.
It is the point in the transaction when the buyer must submit pre- contract searches.
It is the point in the transaction where an application is made to HM Land Registry.
It is the point in the transaction when the buyer must ensure that they have their financing in place.
It is the point in the transaction when the legal title transfers from the seller to buyer.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person has decided to sell their house so that they can move to France. They cannot decide whether to advertise their house for sale on the Internet themself or to employ someone to assist them sell their house. What professional can assist the person with their house sale?
options: The person can employ a surveyor.
The person can employ a solicitor.
The person can employ an independent financial adviser.
The person can employ a mortgage broker.
The person can employ an estate agent.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A school teacher has decided that they would like to live nearer to the school where they work. They have seen a flat for sale in an estate agent's window and notice the following wording in the advertisement: "For sale - lovely 2-bedroom leasehold flat with good views and close to local school. Residue of the lease term: 102 years". The school teacher’s offer to buy the flat is accepted. Which of the following statements best describes what the schoolteacher has agreed to do?
options: The school teacher will enter into a deed of variation of the flat.
The school teacher will purchase the freehold of the flat.
The school teacher will negotiate the terms of the lease of the flat.
The school teacher will take the grant of a new lease of the flat.
The school teacher will take an assignment of the lease of the flat.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor has picked up an attendance note from their assistant which states: “Please telephone the solicitor acting for the buyer of 34 Acacia Avenue, London. The solicitor wants confirmation that as soon as they have sent you the money to complete the transaction, you will send the transfer of the property signed by our client to them today”. The solicitor returns the telephone call and confirms that they will send the transfer as requested. The solicitor on the other side sends the completion money. However, the solicitor is very busy and forgets all about sending the transfer. Four days after the telephone call, the solicitor receives a letter accusing them of breach of undertaking. Is the solicitor in breach of undertaking?
options: The solicitor is in breach of undertaking because they divulged their client’s details during the call.
The solicitor is not in breach of undertaking because they did not use the word “undertaking” during the telephone call.
The solicitor is not in breach of undertaking because the statement was given during a telephone call.
The solicitor is in breach of undertaking because they made a statement that someone relied on with which the solicitor has not complied.
The solicitor is not in breach of undertaking because it is not written down.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a married couple who is selling their house. The solicitor has read the Property Information Form provided by the sellers and notes that the wife’s mother also lives at the property with them. The solicitor talks to the wife and discovers that her mother contributed £20,000 towards the purchase of the property when they bought it 10 years ago. During this conversation, the wife also revealed that she and her husband have had a falling out with her mother who is reluctant to move house. The solicitor has received an enquiry from the buyer’s solicitor seeking confirmation that the solicitor has advised the mother as to her position and further that the solicitor will ensure that the mother signs the contract to confirm that she will move out of the property on completion. What must the solicitor consider when responding to the enquiry from the buyer’s solicitor?
options: The solicitor must ensure that they have obtained the mother's bank account details from her so that they can send her £20,000 on completion to repay her original contribution to the purchase price.

The solicitor must ensure that they have the consent of the married couple to discuss the sale with the mother when they meet her to ensure that they do not breach their duty of confidentiality to the married couple.
The solicitor must ensure that they do not advise the mother as to her position and must tell her to take her own independent legal advice.
The solicitor must ensure that the mother’s signature to the contract is properly signed in the presence of an independent witness.
The solicitor must ensure that they keep a full, contemporaneous note of his attendance note when they meet the mother and that they follow up their advice in writing.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: "The objective is to improve the quality and fairness of negotiations on lease terms and to promote the issue of comprehensive heads of terms that should make the legal drafting process more efficient.": Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS). What does the above statement describe?
options: The Code for Completion
The Code for Letting Business Premises
The Code for Letting Premises
The Commercial Property Standard Enquiries
The Code for Leasing Business Premises
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor has received instructions from an existing client regarding the sale of his house. The client has agreed a sale of the property to a first- time buyer who has not used a solicitor before. The client has asked if the solicitor can also act for the buyer to speed up the transaction. Should the solicitor act for the buyer?
options: No, because of the risk of a conflict-of-interest between the seller and buyer.
Yes, because it is in the best interests of both parties to proceed quickly with the transaction.
Yes, because there is no conflict-of-interest between the seller and the buyer because they have the same common interest in the transaction.
Yes, because the buyer has not used a solicitor before.
No, because the solicitor will breach their duty of confidentiality to their seller client.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is asked to act in a boundary dispute. The prospective client owns a piece of land adjacent to a company’s warehouse premises. The company has recently erected a fence which encroaches onto the land. The solicitor tells the prospective client that the solicitor is on the company’s board of directors. However, the solicitor reassures the prospective client that the solicitor does not act for the company and that the solicitor will keep the prospective client’s information confidential. Is the solicitor able to act for the prospective client?
options: Yes, because the prospective client is aware of the solicitor’s directorship.
No, because there is a conflict of interest between the prospective client and the company.
Yes, because there is no connection between the directorship and the solicitor’s professional work.
No, because there is an own interest conflict.
Yes, because effective safeguards are in place to protect the prospective client’s confidential information.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person has instructed an estate agent to deal with the sale of their property. They intend to instruct their existing solicitor to act for them on the sale. A buyer is found but the buyer does not know which solicitor to instruct to deal with the purchase. The estate agent suggests that the buyer use the same solicitor as the seller to ensure that the transaction proceeds quickly. Which of the statements best describes the appropriate response to this request from the seller’s solicitor?
options: The solicitor can act for both the seller and buyer but must ensure that both receive a client care letter.
The solicitor should decline to act for the seller and buyer due to the possibility of an own interest conflict.
The solicitor should decline to act for the buyer due to the possibility of a conflict of interest between the parties.
The solicitor should decline to act for both the seller and buyer due to the possibility of a conflict of interest.
The solicitor can act for both the seller and buyer if both parties are advised of any risks and consent in writing to the solicitor acting for them.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The Law Society has produced a statement of best practice for conveyancing. It contains a set of steps to follow when acting in the sale and/or purchase of a home for an owner occupier. What is this statement of best practice called?
options: The Formulae for Exchange
The Law Society Conveyancing Protocol
The Portal
The Code for Leasing Business Premises
The Code for Completion by Post
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.1: Introduction to conveyancing: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person has purchased a piece of freehold land from a farmer. It is part of a field upon which the person intends to graze their horses. The purchase price was £42,000. The person’s purchase completed 7 days ago. Are there any stamp duty land tax (SDLT) formalities in relation to their purchase?
options: Yes, HM Revenue and Customs must be notified of transaction and SDLT of £420 paid.
Yes, HM Revenue and Customs must be notified within 30 days of completion although no SDLT is payable.
Yes, HM Revenue and Customs must be notified within 14 days of completion although no SDLT is payable.
No, because the transaction is exempt from SDLT.
No, because the value of the transaction falls below the threshold at which HM Revenue and Customs must be notified.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Two years ago, a person set up a limited company through which they now run their online business supplying water and drainage pipework to property developers. The limited company has not registered for VAT. The person has prepared the company accounts and notes that next month, their taxable supplies for the year will be £92,000. Are there any VAT consequences to the limited company?
options: Yes, the company must register for VAT because the taxable supplies will exceed £90,000.
Yes, the company must register for VAT because the taxable supplies will exceed £85,000.
No, there are no VAT consequences because the taxable supplies do not yet exceed £150,000.
Yes, the company must start to charge VAT at the standard rate of 20% on all of its supplies.
No, there are no VAT consequences because the business is run through a limited company.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A VAT registered development company built a factory unit 2 years ago. A buyer has been found and has agreed to purchase the factory unit for £550,000. The buyer is not registered for VAT. What is the VAT position regarding this transaction?
options: VAT is payable on the purchase price at the rate of 20%.
No VAT is payable because the buyer is not registered for VAT.
No VAT is payable because it is a commercial property.
VAT is payable on the purchase price at the rate of 0%.
No VAT is payable because construction services are zero rated.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A VAT registered limited company is selling commercial premises for £600,000. The company has exercised the option to tax to enable it to recover the input tax paid on the costs of refurbishing the premises prior to sale. The company has found a buyer for the property. The buyer is registered for VAT. What is the position of the buyer in relation to the purchase?
options: The buyer will pay a total of £600,000 for the property under the terms of the contract of sale.
The buyer will pay £660,000 for the property and will be able to recover £60,000.
The buyer will pay £720,000 for the purchase of the property and will be able to recover £120,000.
The buyer will pay £660,000 for the property and will not be able to recover £60,000.
The buyer will pay £720,000 for the property and will not be able to recover £120,000.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A couple are buying a new residential property on a housing development from a development company. The couple intend to use the property as their home. They are not registered for VAT. The purchase price of the property is £300,000. What is the VAT consequence of this transaction to the buyers?
options: In addition to the purchase price, buyers will pay VAT totalling £60,000 but will be able to reclaim the VAT.
In addition to the purchase price, the buyers will pay VAT totalling £30,000.
In addition to the purchase price, the buyers will pay VAT totalling £60,000.
There is no VAT consequence to the buyers as it is a residential property.
There is no VAT consequence to the buyers because they are not registered for VAT.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A limited company has recently completed the purchase of a freehold shop in a shopping precinct. The limited company borrowed £100,000 from a bank which will take a first legal charge over the title to the property. The limited company made up the balance of the purchase price of £47,000, which was paid from a recent sale of a company asset. How much stamp duty land tax (SDLT), if any, will be payable?
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person purchased a property in 2015 for £100,000. The property was purchased as an investment and has been let to tenants for the entire period of the person’s ownership. The person has just sold the property for £95,000. Will any capital gains tax (CGT) issues arise as a result of the sale?
options: CGT will not be payable because no gain has been made on the sale of the poverty.
CGT will be payable as an asset has been disposed of by a taxpayer.
There are no CGT consequences due to the private residence relief.
CGT will not be payable but the seller must pay VAT on the rental income.
There are no CGT consequences because it is a residential property.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person has sold an investment property which they owned. For the entire period of their ownership, the property was rented out to tenants. The person took the advice of their accountant and is aware that they have capital gains tax (CGT) of £7,800 to pay to HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC). Their sale completed 10 days ago. Is there a relevant CGT deadline with which the person must comply?
options: The person must report and pay the CGT to HMRC within 60 days.
There is no deadline because the property was rented out to tenants.
The person must report and pay the CGT by the start of the tax year.
There is no deadline but the person must report the taxable gain on their tax return submitted to HMRC.
The person must report and pay the CGT to HMRC within 50 days.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A couple instruct their solicitor to act on the sale of a property which they have lived in as their home for the entire period of their ownership. They purchased the property in 2001 for £152,000. During their ownership they have extensively renovated the property and their sale completed yesterday. The sale price was £484,000. Will any capital gains tax (CGT) issues arise as a result of the sale?
options: No, there are no CGT issues because the couple are entitled to the private residence relief.
Yes, although no CGT is payable due to the private residence relief, the sale must be reported to HM Revenue & Customs within 60 days of completion.
Yes, they have disposed of an asset which has gained in value so they need to report the sale to HM Revenue & Customs within 60 days of completion.
Yes, they have disposed of an asset which has gained in value so CGT will be payable.
No, the property is not a commercial property, so no CGT is payable.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person purchased a property in 2014 for £210,000. They completed the sale of the property yesterday at a sale price of £315,000. They have lived in the property as their only or main residence for the full period of their ownership but used a room at the back of the house to run their aerobics classes each morning from Monday to Saturday. Which of the following statements best describes whether any capital gains tax (CGT) issues arise as a result of the sale?
options: Yes, the person must report the sale to HM Revenue & Customs within 60 days of completion.
Yes, the person will not be entitled to the full private residence relief due to the business use.
No, there are no CGT issues because the person is entitled to the private residence relief.
No, there are no CGT issues because the owner of the property is a UK resident.
Yes, the person has disposed of an asset which has gained in value so CGT on the full gain of £105,000 will be payable.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.2: Taxation – property: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

prop12.3.stem: PROP12.3_ Preparing the contract of sale_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: The owner of a row of shops in a precinct has agreed to sell the shops and has instructed their solicitor. A number of the shops will be sold subject to existing tenancies, and the seller and the buyer need to discuss the transaction with their respective accountants to agree the VAT position. Which of the following is the most appropriate form of contract?
options: A contract incorporating the Standard Commercial Property Conditions.
A contract incorporating the Standard Commercial Property Conditions. A contract incorporating the Standard Commercial Conditions of Sale.
A contract incorporating the Standard Conditions of Sale (5th edition – 2018 revision).
A contract incorporating the Standard Business Tenancy Conditions.
A contract incorporating the Standard Property Conditions of Sale.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.3_ Preparing the contract of sale_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A development company has entered into a contract to sell a residential property to a buyer.The sale price is £100,000 and the contract incorporating the Standard Conditions of Sale (5th edition – 2018 revision) unamended has been used. Exchange of contracts took place yesterday and completion is next Friday. The buyer is not VAT registered and paid a deposit of 10% on exchange. This morning the buyer’s solicitor received a completion statement from the seller’s solicitor as follows: Sale price: £100,000.00 Plus VAT @ 20%: £20,000.00 Subtotal: £120,000.00 Less 10% deposit paid on exchange: £10,000.00 Balance due on completion: £110,000.00 How should the buyer’s solicitor respond to the completion statement?
options: The solicitor should inform the seller’s solicitor that the VAT rate is only 10% and should request an amended completion statement.
The solicitor should request £110,000 from their buyer client to enable them to complete.
The solicitor should inform the seller’s solicitor that no VAT is payable on the transaction and should request an amended completion statement.
The solicitor should advise their buyer client to register for VAT to enable them to recover the VAT paid on completion.
The solicitor should suggest that their client takes accountancy advice to enable them to deal with the VAT reclaim.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.3_ Preparing the contract of sale_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A seller has found a buyer for their property and agrees to leave all of the dining room furniture at the property. The solicitor uses the contract incorporating the Standard Conditions of Sale (5th edition - 2018 revision) and agrees to draft a special condition to insert into the contract to confirm that the seller will leave the dining room furniture at the property on completion. What are the Special Conditions?
options: The special conditions are the part of the contract which provide that a contract for the sale of land must be in writing.
The special conditions are on the reverse of the contract and contain the conditions particular to any given transaction.
The special conditions are the elements of the contract involving offer, acceptance and consideration.
The special conditions are the small print in the middle of the contract. They set out the detail of the terms upon which the property is to be sold.
The special conditions are contained on the front page of the contract and specify the parties, property and price for the property for sale along with other matters.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.3_ Preparing the contract of sale_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person has agreed to the sale of their property. It is an old cottage and had a large crack in the back wall. The person is concerned that the crack in the wall might deter the buyer from proceeding, so the person plasters over the crack in the wall so that it is no longer visible. The person has not repaired the crack in the wall. Which of the following statements best describes the person's position regarding the crack in the wall?
options: The person may be liable to the buyer in misrepresentation because they have plastered over the crack in the wall.
The person is not obliged to disclose the crack in the wall because it is a patent defect.
The person should carry out a proper repair of the crack in the wall prior to completion.
The person should advise the buyer to have a survey of the property carried out.
The person is not obliged to disclose the crack in the wall due to the doctrine of “caveat emptor”.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.3_ Preparing the contract of sale_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a client regarding the purchase of a property. The buyer has a 10% deposit to offer on exchange of contracts. The contract provides that on exchange, the deposit is to be held as agent for the seller. Which of the following statements best explains the consequence of the deposit being held as agent?
options: The solicitor should advise their client that the deposit is retained by the buyer’s solicitor on exchange of contracts to ensure that the deposit is not at risk in the event of default by the seller.

The solicitor should advise their client that if the deposit is held as agent for the seller and is paid to the seller on exchange, the standard conditions of sale provide that the buyer can recover the deposit from the seller in the event of default.

The solicitor should advise their client that the matter proceeds to a simultaneous exchange of contracts and completion to ensure that the buyer’s deposit is not at risk at any point in the transaction.

The solicitor should advise their client that the deposit is retained by the seller's solicitor on exchange of contracts to ensure that the deposit is not at risk in the event of default by the seller.

The solicitor should advise their client that if the deposit is held as agent for the seller, the deposit can be paid direct to the seller on exchange of contracts and the buyer may have difficulty in recovering the deposit in the event of default by the seller.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.3_ Preparing the contract of sale_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A seller and buyer have exchanged contracts for the sale and purchase of a property. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale (5th edition – 2018 revision) unamended. The property burnt down between exchange of contracts and completion. The buyer is refusing to complete as they did not insure the property on exchange of contracts but the seller is insisting that the buyer is contractually bound to proceed with the purchase. Which of the following statements best describes the position?
options: The buyer is contractually bound to purchase the property despite the fact that the property has burnt down.
The buyer is not contractually bound to purchase the property because is not in the same condition that it was on exchange of contracts.
The buyer is contractually bound to purchase the property but can make a claim against the seller’s insurance for the damage to the property.
The buyer can sue the seller in misrepresentation.
The buyer is not contractually bound to purchase the property because they did not insure the property on exchange of contracts.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.3_ Preparing the contract of sale_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A development company wishes to purchase a piece of land for the purpose of building 20 houses. The development company is unsure whether the local authority will give consent to build the houses and so does not want to commit to the purchase until this issue is resolved. However, the development company does not want to run the risk of someone else buying the land in the meantime. Which of the following statements best describes how the transaction could proceed to meet the buyer's concerns?
options: The company could apply for planning permission and proceed to a simultaneous exchange and completion once permission has been granted.
The company will have to take the risk, apply for planning permission and hope that no one else purchases the land in the meantime.
The company could instruct a solicitor to register an estate contract against the seller’s title.
The company could insert a special condition in the contract confirming that the company will apply for planning permission on completion of the purchase.
The company could negotiate with the seller and exchange contracts on the basis that completion is conditional upon the company obtaining planning permission within a defined timeframe.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.3_ Preparing the contract of sale_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A bank held a charge over the property of a borrower as security for a mortgage loan. The borrower defaulted on the loan and the bank has lawfully exercised its power of sale and has obtained a court order for repossession of the property. A sale of the property has been agreed and the buyer has instructed a solicitor to act on the purchase. Who will be named as the seller in the contract of sale?
options: The borrower’s solicitor
The borrower
The court
The bank
The bank The borrower and the bank
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.3_ Preparing the contract of sale_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

prop12.4.stem: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person has instructed their solicitor regarding the sale of their farmland. A buyer has been found and wants to purchase the farmland for £1 million. At what stage in the transaction will the buyer’s solicitor investigate the person’s title to the farmland?
options: The buyer’s solicitor will investigate title before exchange of contracts.
The buyer’s solicitor will investigate title before exchange of contracts. The buyer’s solicitor will investigate title between exchange of contracts and completion.
The buyer’s solicitor will investigate title after completion, just before the application for registration is submitted to HM Land Registry.
The buyer’s solicitor will investigate title when the estate agent submits the memorandum of sale.
The buyer’s solicitor will investigate title on exchange of contracts.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a client who has agreed to purchase a house that needs renovation. The solicitor investigates the epitome of title which has been supplied by the seller’s solicitor. The buyer’s solicitor notes that the seller purchased the property by way of a conveyance dated 3 June 1992. What steps should the buyer’s solicitor take considering this information?
options: The buyer’s solicitor should prepare a report on the title for their buyer client prior to exchange of contracts.
The buyer’s solicitor should carry out a full land charges search against the names of all estate owners in the epitome of title.

The buyer’s solicitor should raise an enquiry of the seller’s solicitor seeking confirmation that the seller’s solicitor will apply for registration of the title at HM Land Registry prior to exchange of contracts.
The buyer’s solicitor should make a note in their diary that the application for first registration of the title must be made within 2 months of the completion date.
The buyer’s solicitor should raise an enquiry of the seller’s solicitor seeking confirmation that the originals of all the title deeds will be handed over on completion.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor has been instructed by a company client regarding the sale of freehold commercial premises which the company purchased in 2017. The property is in mortgage to a bank which has a first legal charge against the property. The company’s solicitor is obtaining their clients title to the property to enable the solicitor to draft the contract. How will the solicitor deduce title to the property?
options: The solicitor will obtain the title deeds to the property from the company’s bank.
The solicitor will obtain official copies of the title from HM Land Registry.
The solicitor will prepare an epitome of title.
The solicitor will obtain office copies of the title from HM Land Registry.
The solicitor will prepare an abstract of title.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person is purchasing a piece of land upon which they intend to keep their horses. The person believes that the land enjoys a legal right-of-way over adjoining farmland to the nearest public highway. This right-of-way is important to the person because it is the only access to the public highway. The seller of the piece of land purchased it in 2010 and the seller’s solicitor has just deduced title to the person’s solicitor. Where will the right-of-way appear on the seller’s title?
options: It will be contained in the conveyance in which the right-of-way was originally granted.
It will appear as a notice on the property register.
It will appear as a notice on the property register. It will appear as a notice on the proprietorship register.
It will appear as a notice on the charges register.
It will be contained in the deed of easement in which the right-of-way was originally granted.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A landowner has instructed their solicitor regarding the sale of some land. The title to the land is unregistered. The landowner tells their solicitor that the land is in mortgage to a bank and that there is approximately £45,000 outstanding on the mortgage. How will the landowner’s solicitor obtain evidence of the title to the land?
options: The solicitor will request the release of the title deeds from the bank and will register a C(i) land charge to protect the bank’s interest.
The solicitor will obtain a copy of the register entries of the title from HM Land Registry.
The solicitor will arrange for a voluntary first registration of the unregistered title and will ensure that the bank’s charge appears on the charges register.
The solicitor will send a written request to the bank for a photocopy of the title deeds and will undertake to pay the bank’s photocopying charges.
The solicitor will request the title deeds from the bank and will give a written undertaking not to release them pending redemption of the mortgage.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor has been instructed to act on the sale of a property. The solicitor investigates the registered title and notes that the sole registered proprietor named on the proprietorship register has died. Who is entitled to sell the property?
options: The deceased’s spouse or civil partner.
The deceased’s personal representative.
The deceased’s personal representative. The deceased’s attorney.
The deceased’s solicitor.
No one, the property will pass to the Crown.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a client who is selling all their land comprised in an unregistered title. The solicitor has investigated the title and has decided that a conveyance dated 13 June 1972 would be the best root of title. Why, in most cases, is a conveyance the best root of title?
options: Because it would deal with the whole legal and equitable interest in the property.
Because a plan would be attached to the conveyance.
Because it would contain an adequate description of the property.
Because it would demonstrate how the seller became the owner of the property.
Because title would have been investigated at the time of that transaction.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a client who is selling land with an unregistered title. The solicitor has received the title deeds from the client and is about to prepare an epitome of title. Which of the following statements best describes an epitome of title?
options: A document which deals with the whole legal and equitable estate.
A document which is at least 15 years old and does not cast any doubt on the title.
A chronological list of the unregistered title documents forming the epitome, together with the original listed documents.
An official copy of the title from HM Land Registry.
A chronological list of the unregistered title documents forming the epitome, together with a photocopy of those documents attached.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a property with an unregistered title. The solicitor investigates the title when the contract pack is received. The solicitor notes that the only documents listed on the epitome of title are two conveyances on sale. The solicitor also notes that the epitome indicates that the original documents will not be handed over on completion and that only photocopies of the two conveyances are available. What is the significance of the fact that only photocopies are available?
options: The buyer’s solicitor should raise an enquiry requesting that the photocopies are handed over before completion.
The conveyances should be properly stamped and any interest and penalties for late payment must be met at the expense of the seller.
The buyer’s solicitor should request an undertaking from the seller’s solicitor to hand over the original conveyances on completion.
The buyer’s solicitor should request that a plan of the property is attached to the contract to ensure that it can be properly identified.
A photocopy of a document is not a good link in the chain of title and is not acceptable to HM Land Registry on first registration.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a house which has an unregistered title. The solicitor has investigated the title and has noted that a signature on the conveyance which is the root of title has not been properly witnessed, there is a missing plan and one of the mortgages contained in the epitome does not have a receipt endorsed upon it. Which of the following statements best describes the appropriate response to these issues by the buyer’s solicitor?
options: The solicitor should raise an enquiry of the seller’s solicitor to request that the seller’s solicitor applies for voluntary first registration prior to exchange of contracts.
The solicitor should raise an enquiry of the seller’s solicitor to request that the seller’s solicitor makes an application for voluntary first registration immediately following completion.
The solicitor should ensure that the original documents contained in the epitome of title will be handed over on completion.
The solicitor should note the issues on their file and point them out to HM Land Registry when the solicitor makes the application for first registration following completion.
The solicitor should advise their client that the title is defective and that the client should withdraw from the transaction.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.4_ Investigation of a registered and unregistered freehold title_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

prop12.5.stem: PROP12.5_ Pre-contract searches and enquiries_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor has received instructions from a new client regarding the purchase of a residential property. The solicitor has opened the file and has carried out all due diligence and has sent a client care letter. In this letter, the solicitor has requested that the client provide money on account. The client has emailed the solicitor seeking clarification as to what these funds are for. Which of the following answers the client’s question?
options: Money on account is for the buyer’s survey.
Money on account is for the mortgage lender’s valuation report.
Money on account is for the fittings which a buyer agrees to purchase.
Money on account is for the pre-contract searches.
Money on account is for the pre-contract searches. Money on account is for the pre-completion searches.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.5_ Pre-contract searches and enquiries_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a freehold residential dwelling. The solicitor has received the results of the local search and drainage search which the solicitor has commissioned on behalf of the buyer. The solicitor is about to report to the buyer on the result of the searches. Which of the following best describes these searches?
options: Pre-contract searches
Pre-contract searches Pre-completion searches
Post-completion searches
Purchase searches
Due diligence searches
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.5_ Pre-contract searches and enquiries_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person is acting as an attorney for their elderly mother in the purchase of a brand-new retirement flat for their mother to live in. They have viewed the property and it is perfect for their mother as it has a large, communal garden. However, the person is concerned because they think that the land upon which the development is being built was formerly used as a petrol station and they telephone the solicitor acting on the purchase to express their concern. Which pre-contract search will answer the client’s question?
options: The solicitor must carry out a local search.
The solicitor must carry out a common’s registration search.
The solicitor must carry out a coal mining search.
The solicitor must carry out an environmental search.
The solicitor must carry out an environmental search. The solicitor must carry out a drainage search.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.5_ Pre-contract searches and enquiries_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a property and has carried out the title investigation. The solicitor has carried out a full land charges search and has noted that there is a C(i) entry on the land charges search result. Which document in the epitome of title explains this entry?
options: A mortgage deed
A mortgage deed A legal lease
A deed of easement
A conveyance
A contract of sale
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.5_ Pre-contract searches and enquiries_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a property and has carried out the title investigation. The solicitor has carried out a full land charges search and has noted that there is a D(ii) entry on the land charges search result. Which document in the epitome of title explains this entry?
options: A mortgage deed.
A licence to occupy.
A contract of sale.
A conveyance.
A conveyance. A legal lease.
questions.subject: Property Law and Practice
questions.source: PROP12.5_ Pre-contract searches and enquiries_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a buyer who is purchasing a residential dwelling. The solicitor has investigated the title and received the search results. The solicitor has a list of questions that their buyer client would like to know about the property and in addition the solicitor has identified that some title documents are missing and the local search has revealed various planning documents which the solicitor requires. What steps will the solicitor take to address these issues?
options: The solicitor will raise post-contract enquiries of the seller’s solicitor.
The solicitor will raise pre-contract enquiries of the seller’s solicitor.

The MP can introduce a bill in the House of Commons because any citizen can introduce a bill.
The MP can introduce a bill in the House of Commons, and it will be a private member’s bill.
