The MP can introduce a bill but need to get a permission from the Prime Minister to do so.
The MP cannot introduce a bill in the House of Commons if it is not on the Government’s party manifesto.
questions.subject: Legal System
questions.source: SYS11.2_ Primary legislation the structure of an Act of Parliament_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A new mobile phone app has been released which allows users to design secret treasure hunts that they have set up in the area where they live and share them with neighbours and visitors to the area. One resident in a secluded rural village designs a treasure hunt in their area which deliberately takes the user across ground which they know to be dangerously unstable. A visitor to the area attempts to complete the resident’s treasure hunt but suffers life-changing injuries when the ground collapses beneath them. Assuming there is no pre-existing precedent which clearly covers this situation, which of the following factors is most likely to persuade a court that the resident owed a duty of care to the visitor?
options: The resident has voluntarily assumed the risk of harm.
It was reasonably foreseeable that the resident’s actions might cause harm to the visitor.
The resident has greater knowledge of the area than the reasonable person.
The resident acted in breach of the terms of the app.
There is a universal duty for all people to avoid acts or omissions which might cause harm to another.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.1: Negligence: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An employee works as a cleaner in a large office building. The employee suffers burns to their hands from an industrial-strength cleaning product that they were handling without gloves. The employee decides to sue their employer for negligence. Which of the following is likely to be the easiest for the employee to establish?
options: Contributory negligence
Causation
Breach
Quantum
Duty
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.1: Negligence: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A retired factory worker has contracted mesothelioma as a result of exposure to asbestos. Experts agree that their condition may have been caused by a single asbestos fibre entering their lung, but the factory worker has worked for three separate employers during their career, for 10 years each. Two of these employers are now insolvent. What proportion of the factory worker’s losses can be recovered from the remaining solvent employer?
options: Nil, because claims in respect of mesothelioma are statute barred.
The losses can be recovered in full.
One third, because this reflects the solvent employer’s contribution to the risk of harm.
One third, because this reflects the solvent employer’s material contribution to the harm.
Nil, because the factory worker cannot establish factual causation on the balance of probabilities.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.1: Negligence: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Following a road traffic accident caused by a negligent third party, a nurse in the Accident and Emergency department of a hospital fails to use sterilised equipment when treating a patient, and in doing so falls below the standard of a reasonably competent nurse. The patient permanently loses the use of their arm, but medical evidence indicates that, on the balance of probabilities, using sterilised equipment would not have made a difference. What liability in negligence might the nurse have to the patient for thier injury?
options: None, because using sterilised equipment would not have made a difference.
Joint liability with the negligent third party, because the nurse fell below the standard of a reasonably competent nurse.
None, because the nurse was performing a socially useful function.
Sole liability for the patient’s loss because the nurse’s actions broke the chain of causation.
Several liability with the negligent third party, because the nurse fell below the standard of the reasonable person.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.1: Negligence: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A customer has tripped on a loose floor tile in a restaurant and has broken their arm. Expert evidence from a doctor suggests that the customer has a weakened bone structure and would not otherwise have suffered this injury. Will the occupier of the restaurant be held liable for the broken arm?
options: Yes, because the risk of some physical harm was foreseeable.
Yes, because the negligence materially contributed to the risk of harm.
Yes, because of the eggshell skull rule.
No, because the weakened bone structure is a novus actus interveniens.
No, because of the ordinary vicissitudes of life.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.1: Negligence: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A driver is driving in slow moving traffic on a motorway and glancing periodically at their mobile phone. Whilst looking down at their phone, the driver accidentally crashes into the rear of the vehicle in front. Despite the slow speed of the collision, one of the passengers in the car in front suffers severe whiplash and later also suffers from chronic depression as a result of their injury. Will the driver be liable in negligence for the damage suffered by the passenger?
options: Yes, because some physical injury of this kind was foreseeable.
No, because the extent of the damaged suffered was not foreseeable.
The driver will be liable only for minor whiplash, being the foreseeable extent of damage.
No, because damage of the kind suffered was not foreseeable.
Yes, because the driver has committed a criminal offence.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.1: Negligence: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A passenger is physically injured when a commercial flight they are on is forced to complete an emergency landing in a field because the pilot has negligently run out of fuel. The passenger later also suffers post- traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) because of the incident. Despite having no history of violence and whilst still suffering from PTSD, the passenger goes on to kill their partner during a heated argument at their home. What advice would you give to the airline?
options: Your liability in negligence will be only for the passenger’s physical injury.
Your liability in negligence will include liability for the passenger’s PTSD.
Your liability in negligence will include liability to the deceased’s estate.
Your liability to the passenger in negligence is extinguished by their criminal act.
Your liability in negligence will include liability for losses suffered by the passenger as a result of any subsequent criminal conviction that he might receive.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.1: Negligence: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A parent learns that their 17-year-old child has been in a serious road traffic accident caused by a negligent driver, and rushes to the hospital. The parent arrives at the hospital within one hour of the accident, only to find their child covered in blood and in a state of distress. The child makes a full recovery. Whenever the parent thinks of the incident, they feel sick at the thought of what might have been. They also worry whenever their child is not home on time. Which of the following factors prevents the parent from bringing a claim for the psychological impact that they have suffered?
options: The parent was never themself in any physical danger.
The parent did not witness the immediate aftermath of the accident.
It is not possible to recover in negligence for psychiatric harm.
The child made a full recovery.
The parent has not suffered a recognised psychiatric illness.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.1: Negligence: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An employee was working on a cruise ship whilst it was crossing the Atlantic Ocean. Due to the negligence of their employer, the employee fell overboard and their body was never recovered. The employee’s spouse now suffers from chronic depression and cannot work. Which of the following could the employee’s spouse claim for in a negligence claim against the employer?
options: Loss of earnings
Private medical bills
Psychiatric harm
Bereavement
Pain, suffering and loss of amenity
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.1: Negligence: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: During a professional football match, a player performed an exceptionally late tackle on an opposing player. As a result, the opposing player suffered a broken leg. The regulatory body reviewed television footage of the incident after the match. It concluded that the late tackle was a deliberate attack and has issued the offending player with a 12-month ban. What advice would you give to the injured, opposing player about a possible claim in negligence against the offending player?
options: Any damages you recover are likely to be reduced for contributory negligence.
The nature of the tackle goes beyond the level of any implied consent.
By participating in professional sport, you are deemed to have consented to the risk of this kind of injury.
The extent of your injury goes beyond the level of any implied consent.
By participating in professional sport, you are deemed to have consented to the risk of any kind of injury.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A rally car driver invites a friend to join them in their rally car for a spin around a track on their own private land. The rally car driver has been drinking, and the friend is aware of this. Whilst racing round the track together, the rally car driver takes a turn too quickly. The car flips over, causing the friend to suffer a fractured skull. What advice would you give to the friend?
options: Any damages that you might be awarded in a negligence claim against the driver may be reduced, on the grounds that the accident took place on private land.
Any damages that you might be awarded in a negligence claim against the driver may be reduced, on the grounds that you were also negligent.
You may be prevented from bringing a negligence claim against the driver, on the grounds that you were engaged in illegal activity.
The driver may escape all liability for negligence, on the grounds of diminished responsibility.
The driver may escape all liability for negligence, on the grounds that you consented to the risk of harm.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A participant in a marathon falls and sprains their ankle. The fall is caused in part by a failure of the organisers to take reasonable care when planning the route, and in part by the participant’s own failure to take reasonable care when running. The court decides that both parties are in some way responsible for the participant’s injury. Which of the following factors will have the greatest bearing on the proportion of damages that the court decides to apportion to the organisers of the marathon?
options: The relative financial position of the parties.
The relative culpability of the parties.
The number of culpable parties.
The quantum of the losses suffered by the participant.
The participant’s pre-action conduct.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A farmer is training a new employee on how to use a large piece of machinery, and which route they should follow across the field, but fails to mention the need to always wear a safety cord when operating the machine. Later, the employee is operating the machine without the safety cord. The employee is not taking reasonable care to follow the route that has been prescribed by the farmer. Suddenly, due to a machine malfunction caused by poor maintenance, the employee is thrown from the machine and suffers a serious injury. Expert evidence indicates that the employee would have suffered the same injury even if he had followed the prescribed route but, crucially, they would have suffered no injury at all if they had been wearing the safety cord. What advice would you give to the farmer?
options: The employee’s damages will not be reduced because their negligence did not contribute to their injury.
The employee’s damages will be reduced because they have consented to the risk of harm.
The employee’s damages will be reduced because they were also negligent at the time of the incident.
The employee will be prevented from recovering any damages in respect of their injury because they had consented to the risk of harm.
The employee will be prevented from recovering any damages in respect of their injury because they were also negligent at the time of the incident.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Two adults have stolen a car and are joyriding around the city late at night. The driver does not have a licence and is driving recklessly. Finally, the driver crashes the vehicle into a wall. The driver is killed instantly and the passenger suffers serious injury. What advice would you give to the passenger regarding a possible claim in negligence against the driver?
options: Your illegal activity merely provides the context for the driver’s negligence and so will not impact upon any claim.
Your illegal activity means that any claim would be limited to damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity only.
Any liability is likely to be extinguished because you were engaged in illegal activity.
Any damages award is likely to be reduced because you were engaged in illegal activity.
A claim is no longer possible because the driver has been killed.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An elderly person suffers a cardiac arrest and is lying unconscious in the middle of a road. The person has a long history of heart trouble, which is likely caused by a poor diet. A nearby ambulance arrives quickly and a paramedic begins to administer CPR. Which defence will prevent the elderly person from succeeding in a claim for the tort of battery against the paramedic?
options: Public sector immunity
Consent
Contributory negligence
Illegality
Necessity
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A patient with a mental illness is refusing a blood transfusion because they believe that the blood in the hospital has been poisoned by aliens. However, they urgently need a life-saving operation, and the operation will not be possible without a blood transfusion. The consultant assures the patient that they will not give them a blood transfusion, but then does so once the patient is under general anaesthetic. Can the patient or their representatives recover damages from the consultant in the tort of battery?
options: Yes, because the consultant misrepresented the nature of the procedure.
Yes, because there has been an unlawful interference with the patient’s rights to bodily integrity.
No, because the patient will be deemed to have consented and the defence of consent will apply.
Yes, because patient autonomy will override the consultant’s judgement about what is in the patient’s best interests.
No, because the defence of necessity will apply.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: There has been a spillage of milk within a supermarket. The store manager asks one of the supermarket workers to clean it up, but the worker fails to do so within a reasonable time. A customer slips on the spillage and breaks their leg. Which of the following principles will enable the customer to bring a claim in negligence against the supermarket?
options: Several liability
Vicarious liability
Cost of cure
Loss of amenity
Contributory negligence
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A volunteer fundraiser has been tasked by a charity to go door-to-door on a prescribed route of residential streets, to ask residents for donations. The charity specifically cautioned all volunteers to take great care whilst on private property. However, whilst walking down a garden path, the fundraiser negligently knocks over a valuable garden ornament. Since the fundraiser has a weak financial position, the homeowner wishes to sue the charity for the damage suffered. Is it likely that the charity will be liable for the fundraiser’s negligence?
options: No, because the fundraiser is a volunteer and not an employee.
No, because the charity has taken reasonable steps to prevent loss or damage.
Yes, because the charity’s duty of care to members of the public is non-delegable.
Yes, because the fundraiser’s relationship with the charity is sufficiently similar to employment.
Yes, because the charity ought to have taken additional steps to prevent loss or damage.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An employee works as a cleaner in a large office building. The employee uses an industrial strength cleaner without gloves. They later suffer burns to their hands. The employee decides to sue their employer for negligence. Which of the following will be the easiest for the employee to establish in a claim against their employer?
options: Causation
Quantum
Breach
Duty
Contributory negligence
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.2: Defences: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A company owns a disused industrial estate. The officers of the company are aware that teenagers have been regularly trespassing on the site for some time but have so far taken no action to prevent this. A 15-year-old has entered the site and is climbing the stairs in an abandoned warehouse. The staircase collapses under the teenager’s weight. As a result of the fall the teenager suffers a broken leg, and their brand-new mobile phone is damaged beyond repair. The teenager brings a claim against the company. Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?
options: The company has no liability because the teenager was trespassing on private property.
The company is liable in negligence to the teenager for their injury and damaged phone.
The company is liable in negligence to the teenager for their injury only.
The company is liable in trespass to the teenager for their injury and damaged phone.
The company is liable in trespass to the teenager for their injury only.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A customer is eating at a buffet restaurant in a shopping centre. The restaurant is owned by a national chain that rents an open space in the “food court” area of the shopping centre. Whilst walking over to the buffet counter, the customer slips on a loose floor tile which has not been properly secured to the floor. The customer falls over and suffers bruising to their arm. Their brand-new designer jeans are also ripped in the process. The customer had been drinking alcohol. Which of the following best describes the legal position?
options: A claim may only be brought against the owner of the shopping centre.
The restaurant chain and the owner of the shopping centre may both be liable for the customer’s losses.
No claim can be brought because the customer had been drinking.
The customer may recover for their property damage only.
The customer may recover for their personal injury only.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A homeowner instructs a roofer to replace some tiles on the roof of their home. Whilst the roofer is carrying out the repairs, one of the rotten supporting beams collapses beneath them, and they suffered multiple fractures. The homeowner was aware of the rotten beam but had not mentioned this to the roofer. The roofer sues the homeowner in negligence. Which of the following best describes the legal position?
options: The homeowner had a duty to warn the roofer of the risk of harm.
The court will take account of the roofer’s specialist skill when determining whether or not the homeowner has met the required standard of care.
The homeowner did not owe the roofer a duty of care.
The roof did not constitute “premises” for the purposes of the legislation.
The roofer has a claim in private nuisance against the homeowner.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A wealthy businessperson has a party in the garden of their country home. They use an old barn on their land as a venue for laying out buffet tables. Towards the end of the party, some of the guests, including the businessperson themself, start playing a game of rugby inside the barn. The guests have all had lots to drink. During the impromptu game, one of the guests slips on some oil on the floor of the barn, and lands on a rusty nail, which breaks their skin and ultimately causes an infection. The guest sues the businessperson for occupiers’ liability. What advice would you give to the businessperson?
options: No defences are available in a claim for occupiers’ liability.
You can rely on the defence of illegality.
You can rely on the defence of necessity.
You can rely on the defence of consent.
You can rely on the defence of contributory negligence.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The owner of a theatre decides to refurbish its bar area. They invite tenders for the work from building companies and, after a thorough assessment which includes a review of health and safety records, select a building contractor for the work. The building contractor removes part of a supporting wall but does not add anything to strengthen the ceiling above it, because they negligently believe that it is not necessary. The builder also fails to place any sign to warn people of the danger. Over the weekend, whilst the theatre is open but the building contractor is not present, a customer walks into the bar area and the ceiling collapses on top of them, fracturing their skull. Can the customer sue the owner of the theatre for occupiers’ liability?
options: No, because the occupier has taken reasonable steps to select a competent contractor.
Yes, because the owner of the theatre owes a non-delegable duty of care.
Yes, but the owner will be jointly and severally liable with the building contractor.
Yes, because the injury is caused by defective premises.
No, because the customer has consented to the risk of harm by entering the dangerous area.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A visitor to a theme park wishes to cross a stream. There are two bridges. One of the bridges has red tape across it, with a sign that reads “Unstable bridge – do not use”. The other bridge is another 20 yards away, so the visitor steps over the red tape. When the visitor is in the middle of the bridge, it collapses, and the visitor suffers cuts and bruises. The visitor sues the owner of the theme park for occupiers’ liability. What advice would you give to the owner of the theme park?
options: The claim will fail because the visitor was contributorily negligent.
The claim will fail because the sign is sufficient to discharge the duty.
The claim will fail because an occupier owes no duty to trespassers.
The claim will succeed because occupiers are strictly liable for personal injuries.
The claim will succeed because a sign is insufficient to discharge the duty.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The local council is repairing some drains on its land, in a pedestrian area. The council employee has removed a large maintenance hole cover. When they took a break, they left a sign next to the maintenance hole cover which reads: “Warning: Open Maintenance Hole Cover”, but they do not take any other steps to make the area safe. Whilst the employee is away, a pedestrian who cannot read falls into the hole, and breaks both of their ankles. Can the pedestrian rely on occupiers’ liability to recover damages for their injuries?
options: No, because a warning sign will discharge an occupier’s duty of care.
No, because a reasonable person would have been able to read the sign.
Yes, because contributory negligence does not apply to occupiers’ liability.
No, because the warning sign has excluded the council’s liability.
Yes, because the council has a duty to keep the pedestrian reasonably safe.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A boat owner owns an old, abandoned boat which is in need of repair. The boat is permanently moored on the river near a public park, and the boat owner has placed a sign in the window which reads “Warning: do not stand on the boat”. A seven-year-old child is playing close to the boat. The child steps on to the boat and begins jumping up and down. After a few minutes, the floor beneath the child collapses and the child falls into the cavity below. They suffer severe cuts, which leave permanent scars. Is it likely that the boat owner will be liable to the child for their injuries in the tort of negligence?
options: Yes, because the boat owner has not met the required standard of care.
No, because the child is not a lawful visitor.
No, because a boat does not constitute “premises”.
No, because the defence of illegality will extinguish any liability.
No, because the warning sign will exclude any liability.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A cinema operator has inserted a clause into its standard terms and conditions which reads: “Customers enter at their own risk. Any and all liability for loss or damage arising from the state of the premises is hereby excluded.” What is the likely legal effect of this clause?
options: Customers consent to the risk of harm arising from the physical state of the cinema.
The cinema operator has met the standard of a reasonably competent cinema operator.
It will be unenforceable.
Any damages payable to a customer will be reduced for contributory negligence.
The cinema operator has discharged its duty of care.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An events company owns a warehouse and sets it up as a zombie house, where corporate teams can come and experience a live-action zombie shoot-out game as a team building exercise. On booking, the events company asks all participants to sign a disclaimer that states: “The game takes place in the dark and there will be obstacles in your way. The company cannot be held liable for any loss or damage suffered by participants during the game.” In the dark, a participant trips over a foam brick that has been negligently left in a doorway by a member of staff and breaks their watch. Can the participant recover damages from the events company?
options: Yes, because the zombie house constitutes “premises”.
No, because the participant was contributorily negligent.
Yes, because the warning is insufficient to discharge the duty.
Yes, because they are a lawful visitor.
No, because the participant consented to the risk of harm.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.3: Occupiers’ liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

tort2.4.stem: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A water company is digging in the public highway outside of a biscuit factory and negligently cuts through a power cable which is the only source of electricity into the factory. All of the biscuit mix currently in the system is destroyed, and the factory remains without power for 3 days, meaning it cannot continue production during that time. Which losses can the factory owner recover from the water company?
options: Staff wages for 3-day closure only.
Loss of profits arising from 3-day closure only.
None of the losses.
Losses arising from the damaged biscuit mixture only.
Losses arising from the damaged biscuit mixture only. All financial losses.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: An airport worker negligently pulls an aeroplane too close to an exit tunnel, causing damage to the tunnel, resulting in significant delays to passengers arriving at the airport. One affected passenger is on a plane that lands at 5am, but they are not able to disembark until 10.30am. They had intended to drive their family straight home from the airport. However, as a result of the delay, the passenger has no option but to stop and buy their whole family breakfast before they make the journey home. Can the passenger recover the cost of the breakfast from the airport worker and/or the relevant employer?
options: Yes, because the delay is a “but for” cause of the expense incurred.
No, because there is no property damage or personal injury.
No, because there is no property damage or personal injury. No, because the purchase of the breakfast is not a sufficiently foreseeable consequence of the airport worker’s breach.
Yes, because the purchase of the breakfast is a sufficiently foreseeable consequence of the airport worker’s breach.
No, because the passenger was not within the zone of physical danger.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: Frustrated after an argument with their neighbour, a teenager picks up their neighbour’s sledgehammer and smashes their neighbour’s car windscreen with it. However, the sledgehammer is defective and snaps in the middle on impact, causing the teenager to fall into the broken glass. The teenager suffers severe cuts to their hands and face. What advice would you give to the teenager about a possible claim in negligence against the manufacturer of the sledgehammer?
options: You cannot sue the manufacturer because you were engaged in illegal activity.
You cannot sue the manufacturer because you have no contractual relationship with the manufacturer.
You cannot sue the manufacturer because cuts are not a foreseeable type of harm.
You cannot sue the manufacturer because your losses are not financial.
You cannot sue the manufacturer because it was not your sledgehammer.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A gadget enthusiast receives an amateur drone for their birthday. Whilst operating the drone, it malfunctions and falls from the sky. It lands on concrete, and smashes into several pieces, beyond repair. Can the enthusiast sue the manufacturer in common law negligence?
options: Yes, because the manufacturer has fallen below the standard of a reasonably competent manufacturer.
No, because the enthusiast has not suffered a personal injury or property damage.
No, because the product is now beyond repair.
Yes, because the manufacturer owes a duty of care to anyone who ought to be foreseen as being affected by the product.
No, because the enthusiast did not purchase the product themself.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A grandparent purchased a brand-new car for a grandchild. After 18 months, the grandparent paid to replace the rear nearside tyre, because it had a puncture. Unfortunately, the replacement tyre was defective and caused a blowout on the motorway. The grandchild’s car collided with the centre reservation and was written off. The grandchild was unharmed. Does the grandchild have a claim in negligence against the manufacturer of the tyre?
options: Yes, but only in respect of the replacement tyre.
No, because the loss is pure economic loss.
No, because the grandchild did not purchase the car.
Yes, but not in respect of the replacement tyre.
Yes, but not in respect of the replacement tyre. No, because the grandchild did not purchase the replacement tyre.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A customer has found a decomposed snail in their bottle of fizzy pop and suffered physical and psychiatric harm as a result. Which statement best describes the legal position on the issue of breach of duty in a claim by the customer against the manufacturer of the product for common law negligence?
options: The court will presume that the manufacturer breached its duty.
The court will presume that the manufacturer breached its duty. The customer is required to prove that there was a breach of duty beyond all reasonable doubt.
The presence of the snail will amount to a breach of duty.
The court will presume that the manufacturer did not breach its duty.
The customer is required to prove that there was a breach of duty on the balance of probabilities.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A manufacturer has produced a defective quantity of fizzy drinks and supplied these to a supermarket. The supermarket has added its own branding to the drinks, before selling them to a customer. The customer has provided them to guests at a party. One guest consumes several of the defective drinks and suffers food poisoning as a result. The manufacturer is now insolvent. Can the guest sue the supermarket under the Consumer Protection Act 1987?
options: No, because the supermarket did not manufacture the defective drinks.
Yes, because the manufacturer is now insolvent.
No, because the supermarket took all reasonable steps to ensure consumer safety.
Yes, because the supermarket added its own branding to the defective drinks.
No, because the guest has no contract with the supermarket.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A manufacturer of a car negligently fails to properly secure a rear-view door mirror to one of its new vehicles. A customer purchases the vehicle from a retailer. Whilst driving the vehicle home, the mirror falls from the vehicle and hits a pedestrian in the face, causing concussion and bruising. Which of the following best describes the legal position in relation to the pedestrian’s damage?
options: The manufacturer will be held liable.
The manufacturer will be held liable. The retailer will be held liable.
There can be no recovery because the pedestrian is not a purchaser of the defective product.
The customer will be held liable.
There can be no recovery because the pedestrian is not a user of the defective product.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A vaccine has been produced to protect humans against a new virus. The manufacturer of the vaccine uses new technology in the creation of the vaccine, and it passes the necessary safety checks before being released to market. The manufacturer has made significant profits from sales of the new vaccine. After the vaccine has been in circulation for several months, it becomes clear that the vaccine has a dangerous side effect which is caused by the new technology. Many patients who have received the vaccine suffer this side effect. Can the patients sue the manufacturer for product liability?
options: No, because the manufacturer took reasonable care to ensure the safety of the product.
No, because the Consumer Protection Act 1987 does not apply to medical products.
Yes, because the vaccine is defective.
No, because the technology was new, and the defect could not reasonably have been identified.
Yes, because the manufacturer has made significant profits.
questions.subject: Tort
questions.source: TORT2.4_ Pure economic loss and product liability_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

trus6.1.stem: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A will includes the following clause: “I leave £100,000 to my company directors to hold on trust for such of the employees and ex-employees of my company and their friends and relatives, in such shares as my trustees shall in their absolute discretion decide.” Which statement is true in relation to this bequest?
options: The trust will be invalid because “friends” is not conceptually certain in relation to discretionary trusts.
The trustees must be able to identify a complete list of the potential beneficiaries.
The trust will be invalid because “relatives” is not conceptually certain in relation to discretionary trusts.
The doctrine of severance allows the trustees to exclude the friends from the trust and uphold the trust for the relatives.
The trust is valid because case law shows that “friends” is conceptually certain in relation to discretionary trusts.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A client has ordered and paid for 20 bottles of cabernet from a local vineyard. Before the wine can be delivered, the vineyard goes into liquidation. Amongst the remaining assets is a warehouse holding 500 bottles of cabernet, including those which would have been sent to the client. Which of the following statements is most accurate in relation to this scenario?
options: Certainty of subject matter requires that tangible assets belonging to a trust must always be segregated from other homogenous tangible assets and clearly identifiable.
Certainty of subject matter requires that intangible assets belonging to a trust must always be segregated from other homogenous intangible assets and clearly identifiable.
Certainty of subject matter does not always require tangible assets belonging to a trust to be segregated from other homogenous tangible assets and clearly identifiable.
Certainty of subject matter will allow the client to claim priority and assert a beneficial interest over 20 bottles of cabernet in the warehouse.
Certainty of subject matter will allow the client to claim priority and assert a legal interest over 20 bottles of cabernet in the warehouse.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A client intends to leave the following property on trust to benefit their five children: shares in three different companies, a collection of 20 rare coins, two Rembrandt paintings, a reasonable income to support their youngest child through university and the residue of their estate. Which of the following is most likely to be considered sufficiently certain as the subject matter of a trust?
options: My favourite Rembrandt painting to my third child.
10% of my shares to my fourth child.
The bulk of my estate to my eldest child.
A reasonable income to my youngest child until they reach the age of 25 years.
Ten of my rare coins to my second-oldest child.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A client wishes to establish a discretionary trust to benefit alumni from their secondary school. Which of the following statements is most accurate in relation to creating a trust for a class of objects?
options: The lack of evidential certainty will always cause a trust to fail.
The lack of conceptual certainty will sometimes cause a trust to fail.
Evidence of capriciousness will always cause a trust to fail.
The lack of conceptual certainty will always cause a trust to fail.
The lack of conceptual certainty will always cause a trust to fail. The lack of administrative workability will never cause a trust to fail.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: An elderly person, who has been married five times and has had multiple children from a variety of relationships with different partners over the last 60 years, instructs their trustees that they want to leave the residue of their estate to be divided equally among all their children. Which of the following best describes this situation?
options: This is a fixed trust for a class of objects so the trustees must identify a substantial number of the potential beneficiaries.
This is a discretionary trust for a class of objects so the trustees must prepare a complete list of all the potential beneficiaries.
This is a fixed trust for a class of objects so the trustees must apply the any given postulant or is/is not test to any potential beneficiary that comes forward.
This is a fixed trust for a class of objects so the trustees must prepare a complete list of all potential beneficiaries.
This is a discretionary trust for a class of objects so the trustees will not be liable if they fail to identify one or more potential beneficiary.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person intends to transfer their beneficial ownership of shares in their company for the benefit of their child. The person declares a bare trust in their own favour, with the bank as their trustee. The person then phones the trustee and instructs them to transfer title of the shares to the person’s child. The child dies the day after the phone call and has left their entire estate to their child, who wants to know if the shares are included in the estate. Which of the following offers the best outcome for the grandchild in these circumstances?
options: An oral declaration of trust is always sufficient to transfer an interest as it meets the requirements of the three certainties.

Where the beneficial owner orally instructs the legal owner to transfer the shares to a third party, with the intention that the beneficial interest will also pass, the transfer of the legal title takes the equitable title with it and an oral instruction is sufficient.
The disposition of a subsisting equitable interest must be evidenced in writing, according to the requirements of s 53(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925.

Where an absolutely entitled beneficiary instructs their trustee to hold the property for a new beneficiary, this is a disposition of a subsisting equitable interest and should be in writing and signed by the transferor (or their agent) otherwise the disposition is void.

Where a beneficiary divests themself of the entire beneficial interest, it would need to be assigned in writing and signed by the beneficiary, or the beneficiary’s agent, otherwise it will be a void disposition.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person makes an oral declaration that they are holding their house on trust for their child. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this situation?
options: It would be unconscionable for the settlor to resile from this declaration so a constructive trust will take effect from the moment of the oral declaration.

A declaration of a trust of land must be manifested and proved in some writing and signed by the person able to declare the trust, so this oral declaration of a trust will be valid but unenforceable in court.
A trust for land requires completion of the deed to effect the transfer; otherwise, it is invalid.
This is a resulting trust and so it is exempt from s 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925.
It would be unconscionable for the settlor to resile from this declaration so an express inter vivos trust will take effect from the moment of the oral declaration.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person has been diagnosed with a terminal illness and has decided to dispose of their property while they are still alive. The person phoned their youngest sibling and told them that they want the youngest sibling to have their car and they will leave the keys to the car in the youngest sibling’s letterbox. As the person is leaving their youngest sibling’s house after delivering the keys, the person is knocked down and killed instantly. The person’s will left their car to their eldest sibling. Which of the following would apply in the circumstances?
options: Donatio mortis causa will not apply in these circumstances as the person did not die from their illness, making the contemplation of death different from the actual death.
The youngest sibling can rely on the rule in Strong v Bird (1874) LR 18 Eq 315 relating to fortuitous vesting to complete the transfer.
Donatio mortis causa could complete the transfer of ownership so the car will pass to the youngest sibling.
This is an incomplete transfer of ownership so the car will transfer to the eldest sibling through the will.
The youngest sibling can rely on the fact that the person has done everything in their power to complete the transfer as per the Re Rose [1952] Ch 499 (CA) principle.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A parent told their adult child that they intended to give them their champion racehorse. The parent said that they would continue to race and stable the horse, but they would give it to their child at some point. The parent died intestate and their child was appointed as the personal representative of their estate. The child wants to claim ownership of the horse. Which of the following would best apply in these circumstances?
options: The parent intended to create a trust over the horse for the benefit of their child.
The child can claim the horse as it would be unconscionable for the estate to resile from the gift.
The parent has done everything in their power to effect the transfer so the child can now rely on the Re Rose [1952] Ch 499 (CA) principle to claim ownership.
The child can claim ownership of the horse through fortuitous vesting as they have now become the personal representative of the estate.
Fortuitous vesting will not apply in this case as the parent did not intend to make an immediate gift of the horse.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.1_ Creation and requirements of express trusts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A man left the following clause in his will, “I leave my estate on trust to my wife for life, thereafter to my two sons equally, provided they both complete their medical degrees.” Which of the following best describes this situation?
options: The wife has a fixed interest and the sons have a contingent interest so they must complete their degrees before they can access the property.
The wife has a life interest with the remainder contingent interest to the sons. They do not have to fulfil their father’s request to complete their medical degrees to access the property.
The wife has a life interest and the sons have a vested interest in the property.
The wife has a fixed interest and the sons have a vested interest in the estate.
The wife has an interest pur autre vie and the sons have a vested interest in the estate.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: "I leave the income of my shares on trust to my sons for life, thereafter my shares will pass to my grandchildren once they reach the age of 18." Which of the following best describes this bequest?
options: The sons have a life interest which entitles them to the capital of the shares. The grandchildren have a vested interest in the shares.

The sons have a life interest which entitles them to the income generated by the shares. The interest of the grandchildren is contingent on reaching the age of 18, at which point they will have a vested interest in the capital.
The sons have a contingent interest in the income from the shares. The grandchildren have a discretionary interest in the shares.
The sons have a contingent interest in the shares during their lifetime and the grandchildren have a contingent interest upon reaching the age of 18.
The sons are entitled to sell the shares as they are the absolute owners during their lifetime. The grandchildren do not have a guaranteed right to the shares.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: "I leave the residue of my estate on trust to be divided between such of my living descendants as my trustees in their absolute discretion may decide." Which of the following is the most accurate in relation to this clause?
options: This is a fixed trust which requires the trustees to accurately identify the complete list of potential beneficiaries before disposing of the trust property.
This is a fixed trust which requires the trustees to apply the individual ascertainability test to the potential beneficiaries before disposing of the trust property.
This is a discretionary trust so the trustees should apply the any given postulant test to the potential beneficiaries before disposing of the trust property.
This is a discretionary trust and the trustees must provide a complete list of all potential beneficiaries before disposing of the trust property.
This is a fixed trust which requires the trustees to apply the any given postulant test to the potential beneficiaries before disposing of the trust property.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A settlor wants to create a trust over £500,000 to benefit their descendants equally. Which of the following best describes this trust?
options: This is a discretionary trust for a class of objects and the trustees have discretion as to which beneficiaries should benefit within the class.
This is a discretionary trust for a class of objects which will require the trustees to identify all potential beneficiaries.
This is a fixed trust for a class of objects which will require the trustees to identify all potential beneficiaries by applying the any given postulant test.
This is a fixed trust for a class of objects, but the trustees will be able to apply discretion to which beneficiaries within that class should be benefitted.
This is a fixed trust for a class of objects which will require the trustees to identify all potential beneficiaries and establish conceptual certainty of the class of descendants.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A testator leaves the following clause in their will: “I leave my house on trust for my spouse to reside in for life. Thereafter it should pass to my children from my first marriage.” Which of the following is the most accurate in these circumstances?
options: The spouse holds a contingent interest in the house which entitles them to live in the house for their lifetime and then it will pass to the testator’s children.

The spouse holds a vested interest in the house and is entitled to do with it as they wish during their lifetime, including selling it or leaving it to someone else in their will. They are not bound by the testator’s wishes.

The spouse holds a life interest in the house and is entitled to do with it as they wish during their lifetime, including selling it or leaving it to someone else in their will. They are not bound by the testator’s wishes.
The spouse holds a life interest in the house and is entitled to live in it for the rest of their lifetime. Thereafter it will pass absolutely to the testator’s children.
The spouse holds a contingent interest in the house which entitles them to do with it as they wish during their lifetime, including selling it or leaving it to someone else in their will.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A man included the following clause in his will: “I leave the residue of my estate on trust to benefit my wife during her lifetime, thereafter to my two sons in equal shares." The residue of the estate is worth £250,000. The man’s wife has subsequently remarried and wants to give £50,000 from the residue to her new husband to invest in his struggling business. The man’s two sons, aged 25 and 17, are seeking advice. Which of the following is the best analysis of this situation?
options: The sons can use the rule in Saunders v Vautier to instruct the trustees to end the trust and divide the money in equal shares between them.
The wife is only entitled to use the income from the residue during her lifetime and therefore is not entitled to give the capital sum to her new husband.
Once the second son reaches the age of 18, the two sons, along with their mother, will be able to instruct the trustees to end the trust.
The sons will not be able to use the rule in Saunders v Vautier to break the trust.
With their mother’s agreement, the sons will be able to break the trust using the rule in Saunders v Vautier.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: In their will, a person left £500,000 on trust to their child on the condition that the child could not touch the capital until they reach the age of 35. The child had drug problems as a teenager and has just turned 17. The child wants to access the capital of their trust fund now, rather than waiting until they turn 35. Which of the following is the most likely outcome in this situation?
options: The trust is subject to a condition subsequent and therefore the child cannot touch the capital until they reach the age of 35.
As the sole beneficiary of the trust, the child can use the rule in Saunders v Vautier to request that the trustees end the trust immediately.
As the sole beneficiary of the trust, the child can use the rule in Saunders v Vautier to request that the trustees end the trust as soon as they reach the age of 18 and are sui juris.
The trust is subject to a condition precedent and therefore the child cannot touch the capital until they reach the age of 35.
As the sole beneficiary of the trust, the child can use the rule in Saunders v Vautier to request that the trustees end the trust as soon as they reach the age of 21 and are sui juris.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A man has left the residue of his estate on trust to be divided between his four children in equal shares. Following the man’s death it is discovered that he had another child, so the four children have asked the trustees to modify the terms of the trust to allow the property to be divided equally between all five of the man’s children. Which would be the best answer in this situation?
options: The trustees must bring the original trust to an end, according to Saunders v Vautier, before creating a new trust for the benefit of the five children.
The trustees cannot modify the terms of the trust as they are bound by the intentions of the testator.
The trustees can consent to the variation if they have the agreement of all the beneficiaries and all beneficiaries are adults and sui juris.
The trustees must modify the terms of the trust providing the four children named in the will agree, are adults and are sui juris.
The trustees must modify the terms of the trust providing all five children agree, are adults and are sui juris.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person leaves the following clause in their will: "I leave £600,000 to be divided between such of my grandchildren as my trustees in their absolute discretion may decide once they have reached the age of 30 years." They currently have six grandchildren, two of whom are over the age of 18. Which of the following is the best assessment of how the trust could be varied?
options: The majority of the adult grandchildren must consent to varying the trust according to the rule in Saunders v Vautier.
All of the grandchildren who have reached the age of 30 can vary the trust according to the rule in Saunders v Vautier.
The six grandchildren can consent to varying the trust according to the rule in Saunders v Vautier.
The grandchildren would find it very difficult to use the rule in Saunders v Vautier to vary the trust.
Any one of the adult grandchildren can use the rule in Saunders v Vautier to vary the trust.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A testator has created a trust for £800,000 to benefit such of their grandchildren as the trustees may in their absolute discretion decide. The trustees have reviewed the financial situation of each of the six grandchildren and have decided to give £600,000 to the youngest grandchild, dividing the remaining £200,000 equally between the other five grandchildren. The oldest grandchild wants to challenge the trustees’ decision. Which of the following is the best analysis of this situation?
options: This is a discretionary trust so the trustees cannot give equal shares to five of the grandchildren.
The grandchildren have a vested interest in the property.
The grandchildren have a fixed interest in the property which requires an equal division of the property.
The beneficiaries have a discretionary interest in the trust property and cannot compel the trustees to exercise the trust in their favour.
The grandchildren have a contingent interest in the property.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.2: Beneficial entitlement: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

trus6.3.stem: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person owns a company with 50 employees. In their will, the person wants to leave a bequest of £250,000 to support the education of their employees’ children. Which of the following best describes this bequest?
options: This trust could raise problems with the personal nexus test.
This trust meets the requirements of the public benefit test.
This is a valid charitable trust for the advancement of education.
This is a valid private purpose trust.
This is a valid charitable trust as it is for charitable purposes only.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person wants to donate £500,000 to the private school at which they studied. The school charges tuition fees of £25,000 per year. The person is seeking advice as to whether this would be considered a charitable bequest. Which of the following interpretations is most likely in this case?
options: This is an invalid charitable trust for the advancement of education as it excludes those in poverty.
This is an invalid charitable trust for the advancement of education as a fee-paying organisation cannot claim charitable status.
This is a valid charitable trust for the advancement of education. It must demonstrate that it meets the requirements of the public benefit test.
This is an invalid charitable trust for the advancement of education as it is only for a section of the public.
This is a valid charitable trust for the advancement of education. It is presumed to be for a public benefit.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person left £100,000 in their 1998 will to be divided equally between two local musical societies, the Newtown Orchestral Society and the Oldtown Orchestral Society. The testator died 2 years ago. The Oldtown Orchestral Society received £50,000 in the will 2 years ago, but the society closed this year with £40,000 remaining. The Newtown Orchestral Society had never existed but there was a Newtown Orchestra Association. Which of the following is the most likely outcome in this case?
options: Both bequests have failed and the money will be transferred to the Newtown Orchestra Association through cy-près.
Both bequests have failed and the money will return on automatic resulting trust to the estate.
Both bequests have failed and it will be necessary to identify a general charitable intention to transfer the money to alternative charities through cy-près.

The bequest to the Newtown Orchestral Society will be applied to the Newtown Orchestra Association as an amalgamation. The bequest to the Oldtown Orchestral Society has failed and the residue will be returned to the estate.

The bequest to the Newtown Orchestral Society is an initial failure so will require a general charitable intention to apply the money cy-près. The bequest to the Oldtown Orchestral Society is a subsequent failure so it will be applied cy-près to the nearest alternative charity.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The trustees of a discretionary trust have proposed making a payment to the testator’s grandchild, unaware that this would be a breach of trust as they are not within the class of objects. The trustees have instructed a solicitor to arrange the payment. The solicitor is concerned that this is not authorised by the trust deed but decides to make the payment anyway. The beneficiaries of the trust have become aware of this payment and want to make the solicitor personally liable to reimburse the trust fund. Which of the following is an accurate assessment of this situation?
options: A third party is always personally liable if they assist in a breach of trust.
A third party is personally liable if they are subjectively dishonest.
A third party is only personally liable if the actions of the trustees were dishonest.
A third party can never be personally liable as they are not a trustee.
A third party is personally liable if, considering their particular knowledge and experience, they are judged to be objectively dishonest by the standards of the reasonable person.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A trustee of a large family trust had suffered financial losses and was in arrears with their mortgage account. The bank had threatened to foreclose on the trustee’s property so, in breach of trust, the trustee transferred trust moneys into their mortgage account, clearing the balance. The beneficiaries want to hold the bank liable for the receipt of these funds. Which of the following is the most accurate in this case?
options: The bank is only liable if they have ministerial receipt of the money in breach of trust.
The bank is always liable when they receive money in breach of trust.
The bank can never be liable for receipt as they are not trustees.
The bank is only liable if they are shown to have knowingly received the money for their benefit in breach of trust and it would be unconscionable for them to retain it.
The bank is liable if they had constructive knowledge that the money was received in breach of trust.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A client was buying a new house and, on the morning of completion, their solicitor phoned to say there would be a slight delay with the transfer of funds from the party buying the client’s old house and so they would be short £50,000 to complete their purchase, triggering a late fee of £5,000. In breach of trust, the client decided to withdraw £50,000 from the family trust fund, of which they were a trustee, confident that they could repay the money quickly. The client transferred the money to the solicitor, who was surprised, but decided not to question the good luck. The solicitor was having technical problems with their client account, so they placed the money into their personal account. Which of the following best identifies the potential ethical and conduct issues in this scenario?
options: A solicitor will always be held to a higher standard than an ordinary member of the public in assessing questions of honesty and ethics. Juries are more likely to hold solicitors to account in cases of accessory and recipient liability as solicitors have a general duty of care towards the public to act honestly and with integrity.

The solicitor is potentially liable for unconscionable/knowing receipt of £50,000 of trust property. By placing the money into their personal account, the solicitor is in beneficial receipt of the money and has breached ethical standards. Their suspicions about the money suggest they had knowledge of wrongdoing.
The solicitor is not personally liable in this case as they do not have any fiduciary responsibilities towards the trust and did not have actual knowledge of any wrongdoing on behalf of the client.

The solicitor is potentially liable as an accessory to the breach of trust in this case. They were aware that there was something suspicious about the transfer of £50,000 but chose not to question it. In assessing the question of dishonesty, this falls below the ethical standards expected of a solicitor.

The solicitor is potentially liable for both accessory liability and recipient liability for the breach of trust. The solicitor’s conduct and honesty fell below what a reasonable person would have expected of a person with the solicitor’s knowledge and experience. By placing the money in their personal account, the solicitor breached the code of conduct by beneficially holding client money.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person and their partner bought a house together. The person provided the deposit of £80,000 from the sale of their previous house, but the mortgage and title were registered in both names as joint owners, as they intended it to be a shared family home. The relationship broke down 5 years later and now the person’s partner is claiming that they are entitled to an equal share of the property. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this situation?
options: In determining beneficial shares of a family home, the court will only consider financial contributions to the purchase price so the presumption that joint owners are entitled to equal shares can always be rebutted.
The parties are registered as joint owners of the property so they will each be entitled to an equal share of 50% of the value following the sale.

If joint owners do not have a common intention to equally share ownership from the start, or if their common intention to share ownership changed over time, it may be possible to rebut the presumption of equal shares.

In determining beneficial shares of a family home, the court will only consider financial contributions to the purchase price and so the presumption that joint owners are entitled to equal shares cannot be rebutted.
The person has contributed more to the purchase price and therefore would be entitled to a greater share of the value of the property following the sale.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: be rebutted. The parties are registered as joint owners of the property so they will each be entitled to an equal share of 50% of the value following the sale. If joint owners do not have a common intention to equally share ownership from the start, or if their common intention to share ownership changed over time, it may be possible to rebut the presumption of equal shares. In determining beneficial shares of a family home, the court will only consider financial contributions to the purchase price and so the presumption that joint owners are entitled to equal shares cannot be rebutted. The person has contributed more to the purchase price and therefore would be entitled to a greater share of the value of the property following the sale.
options: Equity follows the law and therefore the property belongs to the legal title holder with no interest for the partner.
Paying for repairs and extension work would be sufficient to give the non-legal owner a beneficial interest in the property.
Contributions to the upkeep of the house are sufficient to give the non-legal owner a beneficial interest in the property.
Courts will adopt a holistic approach in determining whether the non- legal owner has contributed sufficiently to acquire a beneficial interest in the property.
Looking after the couple’s pet and paying bills would be sufficient to give the non-legal owner a beneficial interest in the property.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person convinced their partner to sell the large house their partner had inherited and move in with them. The person promised that, even though the house was in the person’s name, the partner could share it with them. The partner sold their inherited property at less than its market value because the person wanted the partner to move in immediately and help look after the person’s young children. After living together for 10 years, helping to raise the children and contributing to the upkeep of the person’s house, the partner has now been told by the person to move out of the house as they met someone else. Property prices have gone up significantly in the last 10 years and the partner can no longer afford to buy another house in the area. Which of the following is the best response in this situation?
options: The partner could show that they had relied on the person’s assurances to their detriment and it would therefore be unconscionable to allow the person to deny their interest.
The partner could show detrimental reliance because they had spent the last 10 years contributing to the upkeep of the house and helping to raise the person’s children.
The partner could rely on an inferred common intention constructive trust between the parties to claim their share of the house because they contributed to household expenses.
The partner could rely on an express common intention constructive trust between the parties to claim their share of the person’s house because the person invited them to share it with them.
The partner could rely on proprietary estoppel to assert the right to live in the property for life.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person leaves £200,000 on trust to their spouse for life. At the spouse’s death, there is still £90,000 remaining of this trust fund. Which of the following best describes what will happen to the remainder of the trust fund?
options: The £90,000 will return on automatic resulting trust to the testator’s estate.
The £90,000 surplus will transfer to the Crown, bona vacantia.
The £90,000 will be dealt with through the rules of intestacy and go to the spouse’s next of kin.
The £90,000 will pass to the residual beneficiary under the spouse’s will.
The £90,000 surplus will form part of the spouse’s estate to be disposed of by their will.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.3: Special types of trusts: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

trus6.4.stem: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person wishes to set up a trust for their three children and wishes to appoint five people to the role of trustee. The trust includes a portfolio of shares and several interests in land. Will the person be able to appoint the five trustees?
options: Yes, provided that the court agrees.
No, there should be a sole trustee where land is involved.
No, there is a restriction of four trustees when a trust involves land.
No, two is the maximum number of trustees allowed when a trust involves land.
Yes, there are no restrictions as to the number of trustees that may be appointed.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A trust was set up 10 years ago by a person for their three children. There are three co-trustees. One of the co-trustees wishes to retire immediately, without a new co-trustee being appointed. Can the co-trustee retire immediately?
options: Yes, a trustee that wishes to retire without a new trustee being appointed in their place, may do so by deed and with the consent of the co-trustees.
Yes, a trustee who wishes to retire without a new trustee being appointed in their place, may do so by deed and without the consent of the co-trustees.
Yes, subject to only the consent of the other co-trustees.

Yes, a trustee who wishes to retire without any new trustee being appointed may do so by deed and with the consent of the co-trustees, provided that, after retirement, there will be a trust corporation or at least two persons to act as trustees.
No. The co-trustee may not retire as this would make the trust instrument void.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person has been a trustee for over 20 years. The person has been forgetting and misplacing things and recently forgot to sign some important trust documents. The co-trustees are unhappy with this and are looking to remove the person from the role of trustee. Can the co-trustees appoint a replacement trustee?
options: Yes. If the trustee is incapable of acting, due to a physical or mental inability, a replacement may be appointed.
Yes. If the trustee refuses to act, a replacement trustee may be appointed.
No. The appointment of a trustee is a lifetime appointment.
Yes. If the trustee is incapable of acting, due to a physical or mental inability, or if the trustee fails to act, a replacement may be appointed.
Yes. As the trustee is unfit to act, a replacement may be appointed.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A trustee decides that, as they have worked for the trust for years, they can buy one of the trust’s properties, a cottage, for the price of £200,000. What rule has the trustee breached?
options: The rule against self-dealing.
The rule against self-dealing. The impartiality rule.
The fair-dealing rule.
The reasonable diligence rule.
The remuneration rule.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A trustee sells a plot of land which was part of the trust’s estate. Because they are a skilled negotiator, the land is sold for £650,000 rather than the £500,000 that it was worth. The trustee takes a fee of £5,000 which they think is more than fair. Can the trustee claim the fee of £5,000?
options: No, this is a breach of the trustee’s fiduciary duty not to make an unauthorised profit and may be a conflict of interest.
No, this is a breach of the trustee’s secret profit rule.
Yes, as the trustee has made the trust an extra £150,000 by skill alone.
Yes, the trustee is entitled to reimbursement for their time.
No, this is a breach of the rule against self-dealing.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: There are two trustees managing an estate. The trust arose three years ago. So far, the beneficiaries of the trust have received no financial benefits from the trust and have received no information from the trustees. Which of the following duties may the trustees have breached?
options: The duty to provide accounts and information.
The duty not to make secret profits and the duty to provide accounts and information.
The duty to provide accounts and information and the duty to distribute to the correct beneficiaries.
The duty to distribute to the correct beneficiaries.
The fair-dealing rule.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A trust has three trustees. One of the trustees wishes to sell a strip of land to the trust. The land backs onto a plot of land already owned by the trust which, in the opinion of all three trustees, makes a development on the trust land viable, and would mean significant financial income for the trust. What duties should the trustees be concerned about and what could they do to ensure there would be no issues with the beneficiaries?
options: This would potentially be a breach of the duty to account.
This would potentially amount to a breach of the trustees’ fiduciary duties and also a breach of the no profit rule for the trustee selling the land.
This is potentially a breach of all the trustees’ fiduciary duties. The beneficiaries need to dissolve the trust.

This would potentially amount to a breach of the trustees’ fiduciary duties and also a breach of the no profit rule for the trustee selling the land. The trustees should seek the agreement of the beneficiaries prior to the transaction.
None, as the trustees will be making money for the trust.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: The trustees of a trust containing mainly land are reviewing the investments. They seek to diversify the trust’s portfolio and are looking at a range of bonds and gilts. What factors should the trustees consider in relation to making an investment?
options: The current state of the trust, the suitability of the investment (both in terms of the type of investment and the particular investment) and the diversification of trust funds.

The suitability of the investment (both in terms of the type of investment and the particular investment), the diversity of the trust portfolio, the need for professional advice and ethical and moral considerations.

The current state of the trust, the suitability of the investment (both in terms of the type of investment and the particular investment) and diversification of trust funds, as well as ethical and moral considerations.

The current state of the trust, the suitability of the investment (both in terms of the type of investment and the particular investment), the diversity of the trust portfolio and the need for professional advice.
The suitability of the investment (both in terms of the type of investment and the particular investment), the diversification of trust funds and the need for professional advice.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)
