questions.question_text: Two trustees decide to invest £100,000 in cryptocurrency. Neither trustee knows very much about cryptocurrency. The trust portfolio mainly consists of investments in land, as well as a large share portfolio in FTSE 100 index companies. The £100,000 is lost very quickly and the beneficiaries are furious. Which elements of the standard investment criteria have potentially been breached by the trustees?
options: The duty to take advice, the suitability of the investment and ethical and moral considerations.
The duty to take advice, the suitability of the investment, ethical and moral considerations and diversity.
The suitability of the investment and the duty to take advice.
The suitability of the investment and ethical and moral considerations.
The duty to take advice, the suitability of the investment and diversity.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor trustee acts as the sole trustee of a trust. The solicitor’s partner in the firm also acts for a company that has approached the trust about purchasing a parcel of trust land. The solicitor trustee has consulted an agent who states that the offer is more than generous. Can the solicitor trustee continue to provide services to the trust?
options: Yes, if the solicitor trustee gets informed consent of all the clients under para 6.2.
No. The solicitor trustee would be in breach of para 6.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct.
No. This would be a conflict of interest and as such the trustee would be in breach of trust.
Yes, if the solicitor keeps the affairs of current and former clients confidential under para 6.3.
No. The solicitor trustee would be in breach of para 5.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for firms.
questions.subject: Trusts Law
questions.source: TRUS6.4_ Trustees and fiduciary obligations_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

will13.1.stem: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A terminally ill person asks a solicitor to come to the hospice to take instructions for a new will and gives clear instructions. The solicitor is satisfied that the person has sufficient mental capacity to make a will. The will is prepared quickly, in accordance with the instructions. However, when the solicitor returns with the will for execution, the person’s condition has deteriorated. They are unable to sign the will so the solicitor signs for the testator at their direction in their presence and in the presence of two independent witnesses. The two witnesses then sign in the person’s presence. The solicitor is satisfied that the person understands that the will being signed is the will for which they earlier gave instructions but considers that the person cannot remember the extent of their property or the persons to whom they should consider leaving property. Is the will valid?
options: No, because even though the person had sufficient mental capacity at the date of execution to fulfil the common law test, the will was not validly signed by the testator.
Yes, because the will was validly signed for the testator and the person had sufficient mental capacity at the date of execution.
No, because the will was not validly signed by the testator.
No, because the person lacked sufficient capacity.

Yes, because the will was validly signed by the solicitor at the direction of the testator and the person had sufficient mental capacity at the date they gave instructions, even though they may not have had mental capacity at the date of execution.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person has instructed a solicitor to prepare a will, leaving legacies of £100,000 to their two adult children and the residue to their second spouse. As a result of an injury to the person’s arm, they are unable to sign their name on the will. Instead, the person applies their thumbprint to the top of the document in the presence of two independent witnesses. The two witnesses then sign in the person’s presence. After the person’s death, questions are raised about the way in which the will was executed. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The will is invalid as the formalities require that it is signed by the testator.
If the testator cannot sign, they must ask someone else to sign on their behalf.
A valid will requires that the testator signs in ink to ensure that their mark is permanent.
The testator’s signature or mark must be added to a signature line at the end of the will.
The testator’s thumbprint is sufficient to confirm their intentions in the will, provided it is done in the presence of and attested to by two independent witnesses.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The spouse of a person who has just died consults you about the deceased’s will. The will is dated 3 June 2015 and leaves legacies of “£10,000 to each of the persons named on a list which I shall write before my death” and, subject to those gifts, leaves their estate to their sibling. A list dated 25 May 2015 was found in an envelope with the will. It names the deceased’s two children and sibling as the persons to receive the £10,000 legacies. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the list?
options: The gifts on the list cannot take effect because external documents can only be incorporated into a will if signed by the testator and witnessed by two independent witnesses, so the sibling takes everything.
The gifts on the list cannot take effect because the list was not referred to as already in existence at the date the will was made so the sibling takes everything under the terms of the will.
The gifts on the list can take effect because the list is referred to in the will, is clearly identifiable and was already in existence at the date the will was made.

The gifts on the list cannot take effect because the list is not referred to as already in existence at the date the will was made, so £30,000 passes under the intestacy rules to the deceased’s spouse and the rest passes to the deceased’s sibling under the terms of the will.
The gifts on the list cannot take effect because wills cannot incorporate external documents, so the sibling takes everything.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person enlisted in the navy and shipped out the day before their 18th birthday. They visited their solicitor with two friends as witnesses to execute their will on the day before they left. In their will, they left their entire estate to their partner. The testator was killed in a training exercise two weeks after they departed. Their family objected to their partner and is seeking advice as to whether they can challenge the validity of the will on the grounds of capacity. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this situation?
options: The will is valid as it was written, signed and witnessed by two individuals. The testator died at the age of 18 so they had capacity at the point of death.
This will is valid as this is a privileged will for an enlisted person so the requirement is that they are at least 16 years of age at the point of execution.
The will is invalid as the testator did not have capacity as they were below the age of 18 when they executed the will.
This will is valid as this is a privileged will for an enlisted person so the requirement is that they are at least 15 years of age at the point of execution.
This will is invalid as the testator does not meet the requirements of a privileged will as the country was not at war when they enlisted.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor has attended an elderly client who wants to execute their will. The client has a typed list of instructions as to how to dispose of the property. The majority of the estate is being left to animal charities, with only small bequests to the client’s children. When discussing some of the bequests with the client, the solicitor finds that the client is slightly confused about the nature of the property and the intended recipients included on the list but tells the solicitor that they must have intended those bequests when they wrote the list. The client has just recovered from an illness and was prescribed a course of medication to help them sleep. The solicitor is a little unsure as to whether their client has mental capacity to execute the will. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this case?
options: The solicitor can assume that their client has capacity as their illness was only temporary and their confusion is probably related to ongoing tiredness.
The solicitor can assume that their client had capacity at the time they typed the list which is the material time.
The solicitor can assume that their client does not have capacity due to their age and appearance.
The solicitor can assume that their client does not have capacity as they have chosen to give the majority of their estate to animal charities rather than their children.
The solicitor should not make any assumptions about their client’s capacity but should consider consulting their client’s doctor to confirm whether they have capacity on the balance of probabilities.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A testator’s will has disinherited their child and left all their property to their next-door neighbour. The testator is blind and so they asked their friend to draft and sign the will on their behalf, in their presence and the presence of two witnesses. The child wants to challenge the will on the grounds that the testator did not have knowledge or understanding of the terms of the will when it was executed so did not have the requisite intention. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this situation?
options: The general rebuttable presumption of knowledge and approval would not apply in this case as the testator did not sign personally. The will should include a clause to attest that the will was read to the testator and they approved the contents.
There is a general rebuttable presumption of knowledge and approval that would apply in this case if the testator had mental capacity.
The general rebuttable presumption of knowledge and approval would not apply in this case as there are suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of the will.
The will is invalid as the testator has not signed the will personally to demonstrate their intention.
The will is valid as the testator had a clear intention to make a will and directed their friend to do so.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A client and their spouse attend a meeting with the client’s solicitor to change the client’s will, which was written following the death of the client’s first spouse. In the new will, the client changed their original bequest to leave their family home to their children from their first marriage and instead left the property to their second spouse’s children. The solicitor noted that their client seemed somewhat subdued during the meeting and their spouse seemed impatient for them to sign the revised clause. What is the most accurate interpretation of this situation?
options: The courts will always find a will invalid where there is a suspicion of duress.
This is an automatically invalid will as the spouse clearly exerted duress on the client.
This is an automatically invalid will as there is evidence of fear on the part of the client.
If the will was made under force or threat of force, it will not be regarded as an act of the testator and will not be admitted to probate without the direction of the court.
The courts will only find a will invalid for duress where there has been actual violence against the testator.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The carer of an elderly testator is an avid amateur actor and a member of the local amateur dramatic society. The carer visited their client daily and regularly spoke to them about the society and its financial struggles. The testator had never demonstrated any interest in theatre during their life. In their will, after some minor bequests to family, the testator left the residue of their estate on trust for the benefit of the local amateur dramatic society. The carer was one of the witnesses to the will. The testator’s family want to challenge the bequest to the dramatic society. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this situation?
options: This bequest is invalid as the carer is presumed to have exerted undue influence on the testator.
It is not permitted to attempt to persuade a testator so the bequest to the amateur dramatic society is invalid.
The family will need to demonstrate that the carer’s influence was sufficient to amount to coercion or pressure that overpowered the freedom of action of the testator.
The court will only find undue influence in cases where the testator is physically or mentally weak.
The carer has persuaded the testator to execute their will in favour of the dramatic society. Persuasion is sufficient to meet the definition of undue influence.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A testator urgently needs to find a second witness to attest to their signature in their will. The primary beneficiary of the will is the testator’s only sibling. Which of the following would be the best choice as a second witness?
options: The testator’s sibling.
The testator’s neice who is illiterate.
The testator’s elderly parent who has dementia.
The testator’s colleague who is blind.
The sibling’s spouse.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A testator prepared a handwritten will but the day before they were due to execute the will, they fell down the stairs and broke both of their wrists. The testator’s two neighbours were asked to witness the will. Being unable to write because of their injuries, the testator asked the first witness to sign the will on their behalf, which they did and then immediately left. When the second witness arrived, the testator then added their thumb print as confirmation of their mark on the document in front of the second witness, who then signed the document as well. The second witness was not shown the contents of the will. Which of the following is the most accurate account of this situation?
options: The will is invalid because the testator did not sign the document in front of both witnesses at the same time.
A handwritten will does not meet the requirements of formal writing and will be invalid.
The will is invalid as the second witness was not shown the contents of the document.
The will is invalid as both witnesses did not attest or sign the will in each other’s presence.
The will is invalid as the first witness signed on behalf of the testator.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.1: Validity of wills and codicils: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

will13.2.stem: WILL13.2_ Alterations, amendments and revocation of wills_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A retired banker is executing their professionally drafted and printed will. The retired banker had instructed that an amount of £10,000 be given to their nephew; however, they notice that the manuscript has £1,000 written on it. The retired banker takes a pen and strikes through £1,000 and substitutes £10,000 in the manuscript, although the original wording remains apparent. The retired banker signs in the presence of two independent witnesses. The witnesses then sign in the retired banker’s presence. Three months later, the retired banker dies, and the executor does not know what to do about the alteration. Which of the following is correct in relation to the legacy to the retired banker’s nephew?
options: The nephew can only take £1,000 because the alteration is not attested with the initials of the retired banker and their witnesses.
The nephew can take £10,000 because the alteration is in the retired banker’s handwriting.
The nephew can take £10,000 if there is evidence from the witnesses that the alteration was made before execution.
The nephew can only take £1,000 because the printed wording of a will cannot be changed by handwriting.
The nephew takes nothing because the original amount has been struck out and the alteration is not effective.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.2_ Alterations, amendments and revocation of wills_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A teacher executes a will which leaves £100,000 to their single parent and everything else to their spouse. The teacher appoints their parent and spouse as their executors. Five years later, the teacher and their spouse divorce. The teacher then dies, survived by their former spouse and parent. The teacher has no children. The teacher’s family is unsure as to the effect of their will. Which of the following states the legal position correctly?
options: The will is valid, despite the divorce, and the former spouse and parent are each entitled to act as executors, but only the parent can take their legacy.
The will is valid, despite the divorce, but only the parent is entitled to act as executor, and only the parent can take their legacy.
The entire will is treated as revoked by the divorce, and so the whole estate will pass under the intestacy rules to the parent.
The entire will is treated as revoked by the divorce, and so the whole estate will pass under the intestacy rules to the Crown as “bona vacantia”.
The will is valid despite the divorce, and it takes effect as written.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.2_ Alterations, amendments and revocation of wills_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: An accountant makes a will which leaves everything to their spouse, with a substitutional gift to their sibling’s child to take effect if their spouse predeceases them. Five years later, the accountant and their spouse divorce. The accountant subsequently dies and is survived by their former spouse, sibling, and sibling’s child. The accountant had no children, and their parents died before them. The accountant’s family are unsure as to the effect of their will. Which of the following best states the legal position with respect to the will?
options: The entire will is treated as revoked – the estate will pass under the intestacy rules equally to the sibling and the sibling’s child.
The will is valid despite the divorce – the residuary gift to the spouse fails, and the residue will pass under the intestacy rules to the sibling.
The entire will is treated as revoked – the estate passes under the intestacy rules to the sibling.
The will is valid despite the divorce – the residuary gift to the spouse fails, and the residue will pass under the substitutional gift in the will to the sibling’s child.
The will is valid despite the divorce – the residuary gift to the spouse fails, and the residue will pass under the intestacy rules to the sibling’s child.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.2_ Alterations, amendments and revocation of wills_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A widower is consulting a solicitor about their deceased spouse’s will. The will was made on 4 December 2015 and leaves everything to the deceased's sibling. The widower and the deceased married on 12 January 2020. A line has been drawn through each page of the will and the words “This is revoked” are written across the top of the will, in the deceased's handwriting. The deceased is survived by the widower and their child, who is aged 18 months. The deceased has an estate capable of passing by will of £200,000. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the deceased’s will? (Note: For this question, see also 13.4.2.1 in the manual.)
options: The will is revoked and the widower will take the whole estate under the intestacy rules.
The will is revoked, and the widower and child will take the estate equally under the intestacy rules.
The crossing through has no effect on the validity of the will and the sibling will take the whole estate.
The crossing through has revoked the will and the widower and child will take the estate equally under the intestacy rules.
The crossing through has revoked the will and the widower will take the whole estate under the intestacy rules.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.2_ Alterations, amendments and revocation of wills_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A testator executed their valid will following the death of their spouse, leaving all their property to their children. Ten years later, the testator added a codicil to their will to include a gift of £100,000 to their current partner. The testator sent the codicil, along with the original will, to the two original witnesses for their records. Following the testator’s death, the executors are seeking advice as to the validity and effect of the codicil. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this situation?
options: As the gift of the codicil will change the bequest to the children, the testator will need to produce a new will rather than a codicil.
A codicil must abide by the same formalities requirements as a will, including attestation.
The attestation of the will suffices to cover the codicil so long as the original witnesses of the will are informed about the changes. The partner will receive the gift of £100,000.
The republication of the will along with the codicil ensures that the formalities are completed through the hybrid document. The partner will receive the gift of £100,000.

A will is a revocable document so the codicil, which postdates the original will, will take effect over the terms in the will. The partner will receive £100,000 and the residue of the estate will pass to the children.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.2_ Alterations, amendments and revocation of wills_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A testator left £200,000 to their sibling in their homemade will. The sibling's spouse was one of the two witnesses to the will. Five years later, the testator added a codicil to their will, adding a new bequest for their nephew. The testator completed all the necessary formalities, asking two friends to witness the codicil, which was republished along with the original will. Which of the following best describes the impact of the republication of the codicil on the existing will?
options: The codicil only affects the clauses in the will that were expressly mentioned in the codicil. It will not have any other effect on the existing will.
The execution of a codicil republishes the will it supplements but the original will is still treated as being made at the date of the original execution.
The gift to the sibling is void as their spouse was a witness to the original will and a spouse of a beneficiary under a will cannot be a witness.

The codicil republishing the will may incorporate by reference any document which is created after the date of the will and before the execution of the codicil, whether the document is referred to as an existing or a future document in the original will.

The republication of the will with the codicil witnessed by independent witnesses will save the gift to the sibling who would otherwise be deprived of the gift as their spouse was a witness to the original will.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.2_ Alterations, amendments and revocation of wills_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A testator left their holiday home to their sibling in their original will. During a serious argument, the testator announced that they were revoking the gift and, in front of their sibling, redacted the text of the clause by blacking out the text with a permanent marker. A week later the testator reconciled with his sibling and declared their intention to restore the clause. Before having a chance to update their will, the testator had a heart attack and died. The sibling is seeking advice as to whether they will still inherit the holiday home. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this situation?
options: Attempting to amend a will after its execution by inserting words, crossing them out or a combination of both will not be effective. The sibling will inherit the house on the basis of the original valid will.

Wills are revocable documents and any amendment after execution will be valid as long as the testator has orally declared their intention to make the amendment. The gift to the sibling has been validly revoked.
The testator had orally declared their intention to reinstate the gift of the holiday cottage in favour of their sibling. This declaration is sufficient to restore the terms of the original will.

Where the obliteration of the original words of the will with black ink is so complete that the original words are no longer apparent, it is possible for the executors of the will to use chemicals to remove the redaction and restore the original text.
The use of black ink to redact the clause to the sibling will be treated as revocation, so long as the words cannot be read using a magnifying glass.
questions.subject: Wills and Administration of Estates
questions.source: WILL13.2_ Alterations, amendments and revocation of wills_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A testator executed a valid will leaving £10,000 to each of their four nieces who were named in the will. Fifteen years later, the testator executed a new will, leaving £40,000 to three of their four nieces who were named in the new will. The new will did not include a revocation clause. The executors are seeking advice about the validity of the bequests. Which of the following is the best analysis of this situation?
options: The testator should have amended the original will by crossing out the clauses and formally executing the changes before producing the new will.
Revocation of a will requires that the original will is destroyed.
The subsequent will automatically revoked the previous will. The three named nieces in the second will can receive their bequests but the fourth neice will not.

The subsequent will only revokes the prior will insofar as it is inconsistent with it. If a testator has more than one will, their respective provisions that can be read consistently with each other will take effect.
The subsequent will has not revoked the first will as it did not include a revocation clause.

questions.question_text: A testator who has alzheimer's was moving into a nursing home. Their children were arranging matters for the sale of their house. The testator had a validly executed will, but the only copy was kept amongst their papers in their study. Whilst packing the study and destroying old papers, one of the testator’s child accidentally destroyed the will by burning. The family is seeking advice as to what will now happen to the testator’s estate. Which of the following is the most accurate analysis of this situation?
options: The court will apply the doctrine of dependent relative revocation to save the will.
The testator can create a substitute will to replace the destroyed will.
Accidental destruction is insufficient to revoke the will as the testator must intend for the destruction to destroy the will.
The testator must make an express declaration that they intend to revoke their will by destruction.
The will has been revoked through being destroyed by burning.

questions.question_text: A testator, who is engaged to be married, is due to go on a skydiving holiday a month before the wedding. In light of the potential risks of the trip, the testator decides to execute their will in advance of the holiday and is seeking advice from their solicitor as to the validity of this will. What of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this situation?
options: The testator’s will would not be revoked on their marriage if they include a clause in their will which states their intention for the will to remain valid following their expected marriage to a specified individual named in the clause.
The testator must destroy their will in order to revoke it upon their marriage.
The marriage of the testator will not have any impact on the validity of their will.
The marriage of the testator will always automatically revoke any existing wills.
The testator’s will would not be revoked on their marriage if they include a clause in their will which states that they do not intend for this will to be revoked in the event of their marriage.

questions.question_text: A person makes a will appointing their two siblings as executors. When the person dies, the eldest sibling is working abroad. The eldest sibling has informed the person’s various banks of their death but says that they will find it difficult to do anything else and wishes to renounce probate. The youngest sibling has not done anything in relation to the administration of the estate. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the appointments in the will?
options: The youngest sibling and the eldest sibling can both renounce probate.
The youngest sibling cannot renounce probate.
The eldest sibling can renounce probate, and the youngest sibling can take the grant on their own.
The youngest and eldest siblings must both take the grant as two executors are required.
The youngest sibling can renounce probate but the eldest sibling cannot.

questions.question_text: A deceased’s will leaves their estate equally between their two children (aged 20 and 25). All three are killed in a plane crash and there is no evidence as to the order of deaths. The spouse of the youngest child was pregnant with their first child at the time of the crash and subsequently gives birth to the child. The eldest child has no children. In addition to the grandchild, the deceased is survived by their spouse and their youngest child’s spouse. Which of the following statements correctly sets out those entitled to the deceased’s estate?
options: The estate passes under the intestacy rules to the deceased’s parent.
The whole estate passes under the will to the estate of the youngest child.
The estate passes under the intestacy rules and is divided equally between the deceased’s spouse and grandchild.
The estate passes under the will and is divided equally between the estates of the dead children.
The estate passes under the intestacy rules to the deceased’s grandchild.

questions.question_text: Ten years ago, a person makes a will appointing as executors their spouse, their 15-year-old child and their accountant. When the person dies this year, they had been divorced from their spouse for 8 years, their child is 25, and their accountant is 70 and says that they do not wish to act as executor. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the appointments in the will?
options: The spouse and the child can take a grant of probate together and the accountant can renounce.
The appointment of the child as executor fails because they were a minor at the date the will was made.
The appointment of the spouse fails but the child can take a grant of probate alone and the accountant can renounce.
The appointment of the spouse and child both fail but the accountant can renounce probate, in which case a grant of letters of administration will have to be taken.
The appointment of the spouse and child both fail so the accountant must take the grant.

questions.question_text: A person leaves their shareholding in a company to be divided equally between their child, their sibling’s eldest child and their sibling’s eldest grandchild. The person’s child dies before them, leaving a child who is living at the person’s death. The sibling’s eldest child survives the person. The sibling’s other child had three children when the will was made but the oldest one died before the person, leaving two children surviving. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the gift of the shareholding?
options: The sibling’s eldest child takes the whole of the shareholding.
The sibling’s eldest child and the sibling's eldest surviving grandchild will divide the shareholding between them.
The one-third share left to the sibling’s eldest surviving grandchild takes effect as a gift to the sibling’s eldest surviving grandchild of the sibling.
The one-third share left to the person’s child takes effect as a gift to the person’s grandchild.
The one-third share left to the person’s child fails.

questions.question_text: A solicitor is invited by the manager of a local care home to give an informative talk to the home’s elderly residents on the importance of making a will. The solicitor gives the talk to those residents who have expressed an interest in the subject matter and, in doing so, presents an even-handed and accurate explanation of the advantages and disadvantages of making a will. At the end of the talk the solicitor hands out leaflets advertising the will drafting services of the solicitor’s firm. The solicitor also offers to draw up a will there and then for any residents who would like the solicitor to do so. Which of the following best describes the consequences of the solicitor’s actions under the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs?
options: None of the solicitor’s actions breach the Code because the solicitor has acted in response to the manager’s invitation and so the solicitor’s approaches are not unsolicited.
None of the solicitor’s actions breach the Code because making a will is in the client’s best interests.
All of the solicitor’s actions breach the Code because they are unsolicited approaches to the members of the public.

The solicitor is unlikely to have done anything wrong in giving the talk and handing out the leaflets, but offering to draw up wills breaches the Code as an unsolicited approach to members of the public.

The solicitor is unlikely to have done anything wrong in giving the talk, but handing out the leaflets and then offering to draw up wills breaches the Code as unsolicited approaches to members of the public.

questions.question_text: A recently deceased person's will appoints their two children as executors and trustees. The person’s youngest child is working abroad on a 12-month contract and says that they will find it difficult to do anything for the next 12 months in relation to the administration of the estate. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the appointments in the will?
options: The youngest child is free to renounce their right to take a grant provided that they do not accept office by intermeddling in the estate.
The youngest child must either take the grant or renounce their right to do so.

Instead of renouncing their right to take the grant, the youngest child can have power reserved, in which case they will automatically replace their sibling should they die or become incapable of acting.
If the youngest child renounces their right to take the grant, the eldest child must take the grant.
If the youngest child renounces their right to take a grant, they will automatically cease to be a trustee.

questions.question_text: An elderly widow has a son (aged 20), a daughter (aged 22), and no grandchildren. They also have a nephew aged 35 but no other relatives. They make their first will leaving their jewellery plus £50,000 to their daughter, £2,000 to their nephew and residue to her son. There are no substitutional gifts. The will is signed by the widow in the presence of their nephew and their son’s spouse, each of whom subsequently sign as witnesses in the presence of the widow. The widow dies shortly after making the will. After payment of debts, they have jewellery worth £6,000 and other assets valued at £322,000. Which of the following is a correct statement of the way in which the widow’s estate will be distributed?
options: The daughter will take the jewellery plus £50,000; the nephew will take £2,000 and the son will take the rest of the estate.
The daughter will take the jewellery plus £50,000, and the son will take the rest of the estate.
The daughter will take the jewellery plus £50,000; the remaining £272,000 will be divided equally between the son and daughter.
The daughter will take the jewellery plus £50,000; the nephew will take £2,000; the remaining £270,000 will be divided equally between the son and daughter.
The son and daughter will divide the estate equally under the intestacy rules.

questions.question_text: A person dies. Their correctly executed will leaves their estate to be divided equally between their son, daughter, nephew and spouse. There are no substitutional gifts. The person’s son and nephew both die before them, each survived by one child. The person’s spouse and daughter both survive them. Their estate is £600,000 after payment of debts. Which of the following statements correctly states the way in which the woman’s estate will be distributed?
options: The spouse and daughter each take £300,000 under the terms of the will.
The spouse and daughter each take £150,000 under the terms of the will. £150,000 passes to the child of the deceased son and the remaining £150,000 passes under the intestacy rules to the spouse.
The spouse and daughter each take £150,000 under the terms of the will; £150,000 passes to the child of the deceased son and £150,000 to the child of the deceased nephew.

The spouse and daughter each take £150,000 under the terms of the will; £150,000 passes to the child of the deceased son; the remaining £150,000 passes under the intestacy rules to the spouse and daughter equally.
The spouse and daughter each take £200,000 under the terms of the will; the remaining £200,000 passes to the child of the deceased son.

questions.question_text: A testator has named their spouse, their 70-year-old uncle, and their 10- year-old child as the executors of their estate. Amongst the property being left in the will is the copyright of the testator’s books. Two years before the testator’s death, they and their spouse divorced. The testator executed a codicil to their will to confirm that their spouse would remain an executor to their will. Seven years after the execution of their will, the testator and their uncle were in a car accident, both dying at the scene. Which of the following statements accurately addresses the issue of the appointed executors to the will?
options: As the testator’s will includes transfer of their copyright, they must appoint a special executor.
The testator’s spouse can be an executor because the testator has demonstrated their intention for their former spouse to retain this role, despite their divorce.
The testator’s child can take the grant of probate as it has been 7 years since they were appointed so they are no longer a minor.
The testator’s spouse cannot be an executor as their divorce means that the spouse is treated as having died on the date of the divorce.
A testator must have at least two executors for their will. As neither the daughter nor the uncle can fulfil this role, there will not be sufficient executors to administer the will.
